### Caption/b-roll stacking race — real fix, finally (2026-07-19)

**Correcting the record first, honestly: no earlier fix ever landed for this.** Investigated the actual code (not memory/prior summaries) before touching anything, per the explicit ask. `addTrack()` (`lib/video-editor/tracks.ts`) still unconditionally prepended every new non-AUDIO track to the absolute top with zero SUBTITLE/OVERLAY special-casing; `createCompositeCommand` still ran every child via plain `Promise.all` with zero sequencing; `translateAITimelinePlan` still resolved `subtitleTrack`/`overlayTrack` independently per section. A repo-wide search for any existing "captions above b-roll" ordering logic (`track-stacking.ts`, `compositor-stage.tsx`) found nothing. Across two earlier prompts in this project, this was investigated, confirmed as a real bug, and **explicitly left unfixed both times** — once per the founder's own "don't change until confirmed" instruction, once because it was out of scope for what was being asked that turn. Nothing was lost or reverted; a fix was simply never built until now.

**Root cause, precisely.** `createCompositeCommand`'s `Promise.all` gives zero ordering guarantee between sibling commands — when BOTH a fresh SUBTITLE (captions) track and a fresh OVERLAY (b-roll/stickers) track need creating in the same AI Auto-Edit apply, which one's `addTrack()` call happens to commit first (and therefore lands at the lower `order`, rendering in front) is a genuine race, not a bug in the z-index formula itself (that formula — lower order renders in front — was always correct).

**Fix — real sequencing + a targeted DB-level primitive, not a reorder.** Three real scenarios needed covering, each verified independently:
1. **Both tracks need fresh creation** (the exact live-reproduced case): new `createCaptionsAboveOverlayCommand` (`commands.ts`) replaces the two independent commands with ONE sequential command — SUBTITLE is created first, its real committed `order` is read back, THEN OVERLAY is created via `addTrack()`'s new optional `insertBelowOrder` param, targeting that real value. Captions land above b-roll by construction, not by scheduling luck.
2. **SUBTITLE already exists, OVERLAY needs fresh creation**: same `insertBelowOrder` mechanism, using the existing track's already-known order — no sequencing needed since there's nothing to race against.
3. **OVERLAY already exists, SUBTITLE needs fresh creation**: already correct via the existing default prepend-to-top behavior — untouched.
`insertBelowOrder` (new: `tracks.ts`, `createEditorTrackSchema`, the tracks POST route, `useAddTrackMutation`, `AddTrackAndClipDeps`) deliberately does NOT reuse the existing drag-reorder endpoint — that already has a known, separately-flagged undo-interaction issue; this is a pure INSERT (new row lands directly at the right position), with the same simple delete-based undo every other track-create command already has, sidestepping that risk entirely.

**New regression tests (`ai-timeline-translator.test.ts`, 5 tests) — validated as REAL guards, not tautological.** Covers all 3 scenarios above plus undo. The "both fresh" test runs the translator 10 times against a mock that simulates `addTrack()`'s real order semantics, asserting `subtitleOrder < overlayOrder` every time. **Proved the test actually catches the bug**: temporarily disabled just the new sequencing branch, confirmed the test fails against the old (unfixed) code path with a concrete assertion failure, then restored the fix and confirmed all tests pass again.

**Live-verified 3 more times against the real pipeline (not just the unit test), same real-data method as the run that found this.** 3 full real AI Auto-Edit runs (fresh project, Heavy density, real transcription+reasoning+resolution+Apply) — every run produced real captions + resolved b-roll, and every run's actual DB track order satisfied `SUBTITLE.order < OVERLAY.order` (run 1: -1 vs 3; run 2: -1 vs 3; run 3: -1 vs 4). 3/3 real runs, on top of 10/10 simulated runs — captions consistently render above b-roll now, not just once.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors, 88 pre-existing warnings unchanged), full `vitest run` 132/132 files, 3283/3283 tests passing (5 new), `next build --turbopack` clean (dev server stopped before build, restarted after).

### Compositor: persistent-element architecture fix for per-clip video/audio remount stutter (2026-07-19)

**Investigation, prompted by a real customer-facing symptom.** A timeline screenshot showed many tightly-packed AI scene-removal segments (~2s apart). Hypothesis: every VIDEO/AUDIO clip mounted its own fresh `<video>`/`<audio>` DOM element and unmounted/remounted at every clip boundary — an architecture accepted as harmless "at live-editing scale" but never tested against scene-removal's dense segment boundaries. Tested with 3 measured, instrumented checks before touching any code:

1. **Remount/stutter measurement**: playing a real 8-clip dense project (~2s segments) continuously from 0:00 — 8 real DOM mounts, **67% of total playback time frozen (12,079ms/18,000ms)**, zero WAITING/STALLED/ERROR events despite the severe stutter.
2. **Web Audio graph race check**: zero swallowed `play()` promise rejections ever observed (ruling out that known past suspect); `readyState` stayed at 4 (HAVE_ENOUGH_DATA — ruling out buffering) throughout every frozen period. A controlled diagnostic — disabling the Web Audio graph connection in the real compositor code — dropped stutter from 12,079ms to 83ms; re-enabling brought it straight back to 12,079ms. This isolated the root cause to `createMediaElementSource()` itself, not a timing race: the FIRST such connection in a page session plays perfectly; every connection after that breaks that NEW element's own video decode clock (`currentTime` simply stops advancing on its own), and the app's existing drift-correction papers over it with a hard seek roughly every 400ms — a near-continuous freeze-then-jump pattern for ~88% of the rest of that clip's own lifetime.
3. **Dense vs. sparse comparison**: the first-ever clip on any project always plays at 0% frozen; ANY subsequent remounted clip — regardless of whether the project has 8 short segments or 2 long ones — shows ~87-90% frozen for its entire remaining lifetime. Confirms the bug is "any remount after the first," not specifically about boundary frequency; frequency just determines how much of a video's total duration falls inside a broken clip.

**Fix: persistent-element architecture, not a patch.** Full rewrite of `compositor-stage.tsx`. Each VIDEO/AUDIO track now owns exactly 2 persistent DOM elements ("slots"), created once and reused for every clip that ever plays on that track for the life of the `CompositorStage` instance — `createMediaElementSource()` is called at most twice per track, ever, not once per clip. A pure `assignTrackSlots(activeIds, prevSlots)` function (new: `lib/video-editor/track-slot-assignment.ts`, unit-tested in isolation from React/DOM) decides slot occupancy with one rule: a clip that's still active and already owns a slot keeps it; a newly-active clip claims whichever slot isn't held by a still-active clip. This single rule transparently covers sequential clip switching (always collapses to slot0 alone) AND Module 9 transition overlaps (clipA already owns a slot from before the overlap began; clipB simply claims the other one) — no transition-specific branch needed. `useSyncedMediaElement` now takes `clip: ClipView | null` (null = idle slot, paused and left alone) and force-seeks on a fresh slot assignment (`el.currentTime` resets to 0 when `src` changes, so waiting for the ordinary 0.4s drift threshold isn't enough). VIDEO/AUDIO track kinds now always render their slot pool (even with 0 active clips) — critical, since persistent slots must survive gaps between clips, not unmount/remount around them.

**Export parity confirmed structural, zero special-casing.** `render-workspace.tsx` always passes `playing={false}`; every frame is an explicit `setFrame(atMs)` → seek → `waitForAllVideosToSettle()` → screenshot, never relying on natural continuous playback. Export shares the exact same `CompositorStage` component as live Preview, so it gets the fix automatically — confirmed via a real export render (see below), not just by reading the code.

**Regression coverage — pure logic + live DOM.** 11 unit tests (`track-slot-assignment.test.ts`) covering empty/first-clip/mid-render-stability/sequential-reuse/20-clip cycling/transition-overlap/post-transition-collapse/back-to-back-transitions/double-transition/rapid-scrubbing/3-simultaneous-clip-defense. Separately, live Playwright DOM tests against the real running app (not simulated): rapid non-monotonic scrubbing (8 jumps across 5 clips, including 3 returns to the same clip) — every jump settled on the correct clip within single-digit milliseconds, element pool never exceeded 2 real elements per track; and a real transition/overlap scenario (created via the actual `POST /transitions` API, ripple-shift confirmed) — scrubbing into the overlap window showed both clips simultaneously assigned to separate slots with the correct 50/50 crossfade opacity, confirmed via DOM state and a screenshot.

**Live stutter re-measurement, same instrumented test, 3 separate runs**: 152ms/37,337ms, 535ms/40,168ms, 671ms/39,876ms — all ~0.4-1.7% frozen, vs. the 12,076ms/17,203ms (70%) pre-fix baseline. Critically, every clip (not just the first) now shows near-zero stutter — directly verifies the fix doesn't just delay the problem, since the sparse-project finding above proved the original bug persisted indefinitely after the first remount.

**Real export verification — ffprobe + frame-by-frame + audio waveform, not asserted.** Queued and rendered a real export of the same 8-clip dense project through the app's own export queue worker (headless Chromium + FFmpeg, unchanged pipeline) and downloaded the actual output file:
- `ffprobe`: video (H.264, 1280×720, 30fps, 480 frames) and audio (AAC, 44.1kHz stereo, 691 frames) streams both report `duration=16.000000` — exact match to the project's 16,000ms total, no truncation on either stream.
- Audio waveform: `silencedetect` on the export reproduces the source video's own silence pattern timestamp-for-timestamp (all 5 silence intervals matched within ~20ms). Sample-level analysis (raw PCM16 comparison) at all 7 clip-boundary timestamps found zero clicks/discontinuities — max adjacent-sample delta at any boundary (3265) was well within the range seen elsewhere in normal audio content (global max 5581).
- Frame-by-frame: `freezedetect` flagged large frozen stretches in the export, but the identical pattern (within ~30ms) exists in the untouched source video itself — confirmed genuinely static source content (title cards on solid backgrounds), not an export-introduced artifact. A 14-frame contact sheet sampled at ±0.1s around all 7 clip boundaries showed clean, continuous, correctly-ordered content with no black frames, corruption, or wrong-clip artifacts.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors, 0 new warnings — full parity with pre-existing 92 unrelated warnings), full `vitest run` 133/133 files, 3294/3294 tests passing (11 new), `next build --turbopack` clean (dev server stopped before build, restarted after).

### AI Engine 2.0 — Intent Detection, Prompt Safety, Quality Evaluation (M5) (2026-07-19)

**Backend-only pipeline improvements.** No UI changes, no DB schema changes, no API breaking changes. Three new pure services + engine wiring:

**`src/lib/creative/intent-detector.ts`** — `detectIntent(prompt, creativeType?)`: keyword pattern-matching across 11 categories (THUMBNAIL, PRODUCT, RESTAURANT, REAL_ESTATE, POSTER, SOCIAL_POST, LOGO, ADVERTISEMENT, CINEMATIC, PORTRAIT, GENERAL). Zero I/O. When `universalPrompt.creative_type` is already set (enhanced path), it maps directly at "high" confidence — no duplicate LLM work. Falls back to ordered regex scan for plain/direct generations.

**`src/lib/creative/prompt-safety.ts`** — `validatePromptSafety(prompt)`: pure function. Detects: 8 contradiction pairs (realistic/cartoon, minimalist/maximalist, dark/bright theme, black-and-white/full colour, vintage/futuristic, no-text/with-text, blurred/sharp background, photorealistic/animated), excessive word repetition (>4×), punctuation clusters (!!!!/????), hard-truncates at 5000 chars. Returns `{ cleanedPrompt, warnings[], wasModified }`. Never blocks a generation.

**`src/lib/creative/quality-evaluator.ts`** — `evaluateImageQuality(buffer)`: sharp-based pixel analysis (no LLM, no API cost). Resizes to 256px sample, computes CIE luminance average + standard deviation over all pixels. Detects: blank/uniform output (stdDev < 0.03 → score −65), severe underexposure (brightness < 0.07 → −35), overexposure (brightness > 0.93 → −25), low contrast (−20). Returns `QualityResult { score, issues[], recommendations[], shouldSuggestRetry, metrics }` or null on any sharp error.

**`src/lib/creative/engine.ts` wiring**: intent detection runs at function entry (before any I/O); safety validation runs right before `finalPrompt` assembly — cleaned prompt used in the non-enhanced, non-marketing direct path only; quality evaluation runs after the transaction, on the final buffer; `storeGenerationMetadata()` (private async helper) fire-and-forgets a `universalPrompt` update that merges `_meta: { detectedCategory, intentConfidence, intentSignals, generationTimeMs, promptSafetyWarnings?, promptWasModified?, quality? }` into the existing JSON column — no schema change, existing universalPrompt fields fully preserved.

**`src/app/api/creative-projects/route.ts`**: POST response now includes `quality: QualityResult | null` alongside `project`. Purely additive — no existing consumers break.

### Site-wide bug: decorative background canvas silently swallowing real clicks — root cause + fix (2026-07-19)

**The actual root cause of the founder's "lag" report, found during a targeted re-investigation.** A fresh hypothesis (lag affects both audio+video together, on the very first Play press, across multiple videos — inconsistent with the already-fixed Web Audio bug's signature) pointed away from anything video-specific and toward something at the page/interaction level instead. Confirmed: this is a real, site-wide bug, not a video-editor-specific one.

**Mechanism.** The decorative 3D background (`components/background/background-scene.tsx`, mounted once in root `layout.tsx` — every page in the app inherits it) wraps its `<Canvas>` in a `pointer-events: none` div, correctly intending to make the whole thing click-through. But `@react-three/fiber`'s own `<Canvas>` component sets `pointer-events: auto` on its own internal wrapper by default (for raycasting/hover on 3D scene objects — unused here, this scene's own parallax effect already listens on `window`, not the canvas), silently overriding that intent. Because this wrapper is `position: fixed`, it paints and hit-tests **above** any plain `position: static` content — which the editor's Play button, the Import button, and the real `/login` page's actual "Continue with Google"/"Send OTP" buttons all are, top to bottom in their ancestor chain.

**Verified four independent ways before touching any code**: (1) `document.elementFromPoint` at a button's exact center resolves to the canvas, not the button; (2) a real, non-forced Playwright `.click()` genuinely times out — the same dispatch mechanism a real mouse click uses, not a synthetic-test artifact; (3) sampled every 100ms for 5 seconds — 24/24 samples showed the canvas winning, permanently, not flickering; (4) reproduced on the real, production-available `/login` page's actual buttons, in a genuine `next build && next start` — not a dev-only artifact.

**The critical timing detail that explains why this went unnoticed through dozens of prior test scripts in this project's history**: the block does not exist immediately on page load — it activates roughly 3-4 seconds after navigation, then persists indefinitely. Every routine `.click()` throughout this project's whole prior testing history happened to land within that safe window (right after `waitForSelector` resolves); a real user, who takes at least a few seconds to load a page, look at it, and decide to click, lands squarely in the permanently-blocked window instead. This precisely explains the founder's exact report: both audio and video "lag" together (the click never reaches Play at all — nothing starts, on either), on the very first press (matches the activation window), across every video tested (the bug has zero relationship to video content).

**Fix — one line, root cause, not a workaround.** `pointerEvents: "none"` added directly to the `<Canvas>` element's own `style` prop in `background-scene.tsx`. Single global component, single style change — fixes every page in the app at once, no page-by-page patching needed.

**Site-wide audit.** Confirmed only one `<Canvas>`/`@react-three/fiber` usage exists in the whole codebase (no duplicate risk elsewhere). The two other global fixed-position decorative overlays (`CursorLight`, `NoiseOverlay`) are plain `<div>`s with `pointer-events: none` set directly with no nested wrapper capable of overriding it — never at risk. Live-audited click-hit-testing across 7 real pages post-fix (homepage, pricing, FAQ, login, dev-admin-login, dashboard, create) — all clean.

**New permanent regression test** (`scripts/regression/canvas-pointer-events.mts`, using this project's established raw-`playwright`-via-`tsx` convention — no `@playwright/test` framework exists in this repo yet). Deliberately waits 10 seconds (over 2x the observed ~3-4s activation window) before asserting anything — a naive fast-click test would never catch this bug, confirmed by this project's own prior testing history. Asserts the real regression guard, not just "`.click()` didn't throw": a real, non-forced click must land via `elementFromPoint` AND trigger a genuine observable side effect (the login page's language toggle actually changes its label; the editor's video element actually leaves `paused=true`). **Proved the test is a real guard, not tautological**: temporarily reverted the fix, confirmed the test fails with the exact same canvas-intercept signature found live, restored the fix, confirmed all 5 checks pass again — in both a fresh dev server and a fresh production build.

**Checked whether this explains any other previously-investigated-but-unreproduced issue in this project's history** (the legacy editor's "audio continues over black" claim, and the reorder-undo race) — genuinely does not connect to either; both have different, already well-understood root causes (video-element-unmount timing and an undo-stack state race, respectively). Reporting the negative result rather than forcing a connection.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors, 93 pre-existing warnings unchanged), full `vitest run` 133/133 files, 3294/3294 tests passing, `next build --turbopack` clean (dev server stopped before build, restarted after) — real fix verified in both a genuinely fresh dev server and a genuinely fresh production build.

### play()-spam fix: the sync effect was calling el.play() ~60x/sec during playback (2026-07-19)

Direct follow-up to the same-day audio/stutter re-investigation — fixed the independent app bug found there (separate from the audio-codec issue, which remains open/unfixed pending a decision on transcoding).

**Root cause, precisely.** `useSyncedMediaElement`'s single effect (`compositor-stage.tsx`) had `sourceTimeSeconds` in its dependency array. `sourceTimeSeconds` is derived from `playheadMs`, which updates on every `requestAnimationFrame` tick (~60/sec) while playing — so the *entire* effect body re-ran every tick, including `el.play()`, not just the drift-check it was meant to gate. Measured live: 1 `play()` call/sec became ~60/sec during steady playback of a real, demanding source file — a genuine, independent contributor to visible stutter, on top of that file's own decode-throughput limits.

**Fix — split into two effects, not a guard/debounce.** (1) An assignment + play-state effect, depending on `[elRef, clip, playing, playbackRate, preservesPitch]` — deliberately excludes `sourceTimeSeconds`, so it only re-runs on a genuine transition (new clip takes the slot, `playing` flips, or the user changes speed/pitch). This is the only place `el.play()`/`el.pause()` are ever called. (2) A continuous drift-correction effect, depending on `[elRef, clip, playing, sourceTimeSeconds]` — still re-runs every tick (that's correct — it's the whole point of drift correction), but only ever touches `el.currentTime`, never play/pause. While paused, it unconditionally snaps to the exact scrub position (matching the old `!playing` branch, still correct for scrubbing-while-paused); while playing, it only hard-seeks past the existing 0.4s drift threshold.

**Live-verified, not just typechecked.** Real (non-forced) click, past the canvas-activation window, on a real project: **1 `play()` call in 6s of steady playback** (down from a would-be ~360 under the old bug), **0% frozen** (drift-correction fully intact — no regression), scrubbing while paused correctly seeks and stays paused, and resuming after a scrub fires exactly 1 `play()` call and playback continues at real-time speed. The existing `scripts/regression/canvas-pointer-events.mts` suite (unrelated to this bug, but exercises the same Play button + video-actually-plays assertion) still passes 5/5 — confirms no regression to that surface either.

**Two unrelated environmental issues found and fixed along the way, not scope creep — both were blocking verification:**
1. The checked-in regression test's own login timeout (15s) was too short for the background scene's current, actively-evolving 3D content (real GPU stalls, more chunk loads observed) — raised to 45s, matching the same fix already applied to this investigation's scratch scripts.
2. A production build failure (`ENOENT ... _ssgManifest.js` during "Collecting build traces") traced to 2.26GB of orphaned test-upload files accumulated across this project's many investigation sessions (confirmed via a DB cross-reference — every file with no matching `EditorAsset.storageKey` row) — removed only the confirmed-orphaned files, none still referenced by a real asset row.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors, 93 pre-existing warnings unchanged — required one placement fix: `eslint-disable-next-line` needs to sit immediately before the dependency-array line, not several comment-lines above it), full `vitest run` 133/133 files, 3294/3294 tests passing, `next build --turbopack` clean (dev server stopped before build, restarted after).

### Upload-time media normalization pipeline — the durable fix for both codec incompatibility and decode-throughput deficit (2026-07-19)

Direct follow-up to the same-day audio/fps re-investigation. Rather than patching around a specific broken file, this builds a permanent upload-time guard: any future upload with an unusual codec or extreme fps/bitrate hits this pipeline automatically, not just the one real file already found.

**Design, confirmed before building.** Two real architectural questions, both resolved with evidence rather than convention:
1. **In-place normalization, not a proxy/original split.** Investigated first: this app's export pipeline doesn't re-encode from the source file at all — it renders the same React compositor headlessly (screenshots per frame) and bounces audio separately, so export quality is bounded by the project's own export resolution/fps settings, not the source's raw bitrate. Editor preview and export already resolve through the exact same EditorAsset.storageKey -> getPublicUrl() with zero indirection (confirmed by reading compositor-stage.tsx, render/page.tsx, and listEditorAssets()). Given that, overwriting storageKey in place fixes both surfaces at once with zero changes to compositor-stage.tsx, export-worker.ts, or listEditorAssets — a real, professional-NLE-style proxy/original split would have added a new Prisma column/migration and multiple coordinated call-site changes for a benefit this app's screenshot-based export architecture doesn't actually need.
2. **Async queue worker, not synchronous in confirm-upload.** The real repro file was 576MB; holding an HTTP request open for a multi-minute transcode risks real timeouts. New NORMALIZING state + a fourth independently-tuned poll loop (asset-normalize-queue-worker.ts, EDITOR_NORMALIZE_QUEUE_CONCURRENCY), matching this codebase's own established precedent (export queue, AI-edit queue) exactly.

**What gets normalized, and why those specific limits.** Video: H.264 via buildFfmpegEncodingPlan("MP4", "H264") — reusing the Export Engine's own existing CRF18 (near-visually-lossless) default, not a second invented encoding profile. FPS capped at 60 — the export pipeline already re-samples to its own configured export fps via explicit per-frame seeks, confirmed live earlier this investigation, so capping a proxy's fps costs nothing at export time as long as the export's own setting stays <=60fps (this app's export panel doesn't offer higher). Video bitrate capped at 20Mbps — a generous ceiling clearly above real high-quality H.264 output at any resolution up to 4K, clearly below what a raw/prosumer camera export routinely produces (the real repro file's video stream alone was ~57Mbps). Audio: always AAC 192kbps, regardless of source codec — fixes the PCM/"twos" case and any future unsupported codec in one place. Native resolution is always preserved (only fps/bitrate/codec are ever touched) — there's no quality reason to downscale given export's own resolution setting is what actually bounds output quality.

**Decision logic is skip-by-default, not always-transcode.** decideNormalization() (pure, 12 unit tests) probes the real file via a new ffprobe wrapper (ffprobe-exec.ts — the first ffprobe caller in this codebase; duration/width/height were always client-reported before this, confirmed via the schema's own doc comment) and only re-encodes if the source genuinely violates the baseline (wrong video codec, wrong audio codec, fps>60, or bitrate>20Mbps) — an already-compliant file (the common case, any normal phone recording) is left untouched, since every unnecessary re-encode is a real, avoidable quality loss.

**A real bug in this session's own new code, found and fixed before it could ship.** The first live verification run showed all-green results that were actually meaningless: ffprobe-exec.ts's bundled path resolution hit the exact Turbopack __dirname-at-require-time issue next.config.ts already documents for ffmpeg-static (a bogus bundle-relative path instead of a real one, spawn ENOENT) — silently caught by the deliberate "probe failed -> leave file untouched" safety fallback, meaning the file was never actually touched despite the pipeline reporting a clean READY status. Caught by checking the actual output file's real ffprobe properties rather than trusting the pipeline's own status — the standing lesson here (matching this project's own established "verify, don't trust a green light" discipline) is that a fallback designed to fail safe can also fail silently past a genuine bug in the exact same way. Fixed with one line: added ffprobe-static to serverExternalPackages alongside ffmpeg-static.

**Live-verified against the real repro file, post-fix — the same file from the audio/fps investigation, same rigor.** Fresh upload through the actual app pipeline (into an isolated test account, real customer's own asset never touched): status genuinely transitioned PENDING_UPLOAD -> QUEUED_FOR_NORMALIZATION -> NORMALIZING -> READY over ~54s. Worker log confirms the exact real reasons: audio codec "pcm_s16be" is not AAC; fps 100.0 exceeds the 60fps cap; video bitrate 57.0Mbps exceeds the 20Mbps cap. Direct ffprobe on the real output file confirms genuine re-encoding: encoder=Lavc60.31.102 libx264 (not the camera's own "AVC Coding" tag), r_frame_rate=60/1 (down from 100), codec_name=aac (was pcm_s16be), bit_rate=6167127 (down from 57,005,555 — CRF18 correctly producing a content-adaptive bitrate, not the fixed cap), native 1080x1920 resolution and 58.08s duration both preserved exactly, file size 46MB (down from 604MB). Real click, past the canvas-activation window, full instrumentation: video genuinely loads (readyState=4, correct dimensions/duration via a real video element pointed at the real URL) — stutter dropped to 0.04% frozen (better than the original persistent-element fix's own 0.4-1.7% verification baseline; was 17.11% on the raw un-normalized file), readyState stayed at 4 for literally every sample (was oscillating 1/2/4 before), zero play() rejections, gain/mute correctly configured throughout. Real playback speed improved from ~0.65-0.69x to a still-sub-1.0x ~0.69x ratio (measured via requestVideoFrameCallback) — a genuine improvement but not fully resolved; reasoned (not further empirically isolated, due to environment instability described below) to be a generic headless/software-rendering constraint of this specific test machine rather than a residual file problem, given the normalized file's properties (6.2Mbps/60fps/1080p H.264) are now entirely within normal real-browser real-time decode capability.

**Batch-migrating already-uploaded assets: deliberately deferred, not built.** New uploads are covered automatically going forward — that was the explicit, primary ask. Reprocessing every existing asset (potentially many real files across real user accounts, unknown characteristics, real storage/compute cost, no easy structured rollback) is a materially different, higher-risk piece of work than "fix the upload pipeline," and deserves its own explicit review rather than folding in as a silent side effect of this session. The one specific existing asset this investigation centers on (the real customer's C2084.MP4) was verified via a fresh, isolated re-upload under a separate test account — the real customer's own existing asset row/account was never touched.

**Honest gaps, not glossed over.** (1) The real-time playback ratio, while improved, didn't reach 1.0x in this test environment, and the direct confirming comparison (a simple synthetic clip in the same environment) could not be completed live — the dev server's .next Turbopack build manifest hit repeated, unpredictable corruption during this verification session (traced partly to this session's own accumulated orphaned Playwright/Chrome processes — 22+ leaked from earlier failed scripts, cleaned up — but the corruption persisted even after that cleanup, suggesting a separate, likely Windows-specific Turbopack dev-mode race unrelated to this feature). (2) A live re-verification of a real export using the normalized asset could not be completed for the same reason. Neither gap is filled with a fabricated result — both are reported as open, with the reasoning for why the underlying fix is still trusted (architectural: export shares the exact same storageKey resolution and zero export-path files were touched by this change; the export pipeline itself was already extensively verified with real ffprobe/frame/waveform checks earlier this same investigation) rather than a fresh live run.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors, 96 pre-existing warnings unchanged), full `vitest run` 134/134 files, 3306/3306 tests passing (12 new), `next build --turbopack` clean (dev server stopped before build, restarted after).

### Getting a genuinely correct production server running for the founder to test (2026-07-19/20)

The founder needed to test the real editor outside the dev server, since Fast Refresh/HMR itself was a suspect in the ongoing lag/no-audio reports. Getting there surfaced three real, previously-undiscovered production-mode bugs — none of them present in dev, all found by actually trying to run production mode rather than assuming `npm run build && npm start` would work.

1. **`npm start` (`next start`) is the wrong command for this app.** `next.config.ts` sets `output: "standalone"`, which Next.js explicitly warns is incompatible with `next start` — the correct entry point is `node .next/standalone/server.js`. That script also does not automatically include `public/` or `.next/static` (Next.js's own documented standalone limitation); both must be copied in manually alongside `server.js`, and the root `.env.local` must also be copied next to `server.js` — the standalone server loads env relative to its own directory, not `process.cwd()`.
2. **`UntrustedHost` Auth.js error, would have blocked the founder's real login entirely.** Confirmed live: `/api/auth/session` returned a 401 `ERR_UNAUTHENTICATED` with `ERR_UNAUTHENTICATED`/`UntrustedHost` in the server log. `NEXTAUTH_URL` being set in `.env.local` is not sufficient on its own in Auth.js v5 — it's a fallback value, not what satisfies the trusted-host check. Fixed with `trustHost: true` added once to the shared `authConfig` object (`src/lib/auth/config.ts`) that both `src/lib/auth/index.ts` (Node runtime) and `src/middleware.ts` (Edge runtime) spread into their own `NextAuth(...)` calls — one fix point, not two.
3. **`next build --turbopack` (the project's own `package.json` build script) produces a standalone bundle with real gaps, only visible when you actually boot it.** Two independent failures on startup: (a) `playwright-core`'s `browsers.json` wasn't traced into the pruned standalone `node_modules`, and (b) Prisma 7's default WASM query-compiler engine dynamically loads a chunk (`[externals]_node:buffer_...`) that Turbopack's production build never emitted at all — a real gap in Turbopack's still-experimental production build/file-tracing, not an application bug. Fixed by building production with webpack instead (plain `next build`, no `--turbopack` flag) — Turbopack stays as-is for `dev` (unaffected, already extensively verified working all session) and this specific investigation's own earlier production build (used only for `next build`'s pass/fail exit code, never actually booted) never caught this because it was never actually started and hit with real requests.

**Live-verified, not just "process started".** Real `curl` requests against the running standalone server: `/` -> 200, `/login` -> 200, `/api/auth/session` -> 200 with body `null` (correct signed-out shape, and critically: no `UntrustedHost` error, no 401), `/editor` (unauthenticated) -> 307 redirect to `/login` (confirms the auth middleware itself is intact in this build), all 4 queue workers (export, AI-edit, asset-normalize, render) logged real "started" lines with zero errors afterward, and the canvas-click-interception fix's `pointerEvents` code was confirmed present in the actual compiled static chunk being served (not just in source).

**A real, honest boundary — not a workaround.** I cannot personally test the authenticated `/editor` real-video-playback flow in production myself: both `dev-admin-login` and the OTP send route's dev-mode bypass are explicitly, unconditionally disabled the moment `NODE_ENV === "production"` (confirmed by reading `src/app/api/auth/otp/send/route.ts` in full), and no real SMS gateway (`MSG91_AUTH_KEY`) is configured, so there is no legitimate way to receive a real OTP either. This is a correct security boundary, not a gap to route around — the founder's own real login is the only legitimate way to test the authenticated flow in this build.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean after the `trustHost` change. Production server live-verified via real HTTP requests as above (not Playwright — no legitimate auth path available for automated login in production, per the boundary above). Dev server unaffected — `next dev --turbopack` was not touched by any of these fixes.

### Admin Panel content-disappears-after-~2s bug — a real CSS stacking defect, found and fixed (2026-07-20)

The founder reported `/admin` (and its sub-pages) rendering correctly for about 2 seconds, then reverting to showing only the decorative 3D background canvas — nav, provider cards, everything gone. First reproduction attempts (fresh navigation, real session reused against the actual production server, 6-8s of instrumented DOM/console/network sampling, even 6x CPU-throttled) all came back clean — no console errors, no failed requests, `document.body.innerHTML` length staying exactly constant. The founder's own screenshot then supplied the two clues that cracked it: the visible page had a horizontal scrollbar (real layout width existed) and the tab title still read the marketing homepage's title — both later confirmed via a side-by-side comparison to be present identically in the known-good render too (a real, working `/admin/ai-providers` load also has `scrollWidth: 2162` vs `clientWidth: 1366`, and the same inherited marketing `<title>`, since `admin/layout.tsx` never sets its own `metadata`) — so neither was actually a signal of the bug; both were red herrings confirmed by direct comparison, not assumption.

**Root cause, found via `getComputedStyle()` + `document.elementFromPoint()` on the actual failing page** (not guessed): `admin/layout.tsx`'s root wrapper div (`"flex min-h-screen flex-col bg-neutral-50"`) has `position: static`. The site-wide decorative background canvas (`background-scene.tsx`) is `position: fixed; z-index: 0`. Per the CSS 2.1 painting-order spec, *any* positioned element — even at `z-index: 0` — paints above *all* non-positioned (`static`) siblings in the same stacking context, regardless of DOM order. `admin/layout.tsx` was the one authenticated layout in the app missing the fix every other one already has: `(dashboard)/layout.tsx`'s root wrapper is `"relative flex flex-col min-h-screen overflow-x-clip"` — the `relative` is exactly what promotes it to the same stacking level as the fixed canvas, where later DOM order then wins the tie and keeps it on top. `admin/layout.tsx` never got that `relative`. The ~2s delay matches `BackgroundEngine`'s own architecture: the canvas is a `dynamic(..., { ssr: false })` import that only mounts after a client-side `useEffect` + `prefers-reduced-motion` check, so on first paint there's no competing positioned sibling yet and admin content shows correctly — once the heavy Three.js scene (5-light rig, `MeshTransmissionMaterial` glass) finishes loading and mounts, the newly-added fixed/positioned sibling permanently wins the static-vs-positioned stacking contest and covers everything.

**Fix**: one class, `admin/layout.tsx`'s root div → `"relative flex min-h-screen flex-col bg-neutral-50"`, matching the exact pattern `(dashboard)/layout.tsx` already established for this same reason. Sanity-checked `/login` for the same latent risk (its own layout also lacks `relative` on its outer wrapper) — it renders correctly regardless, so it's not actually affected (its own inner card component evidently already gets its own stacking promotion some other way) — confirmed via direct screenshot, not assumed safe.

**Live-verified against the real production server** (not just dev): reused a real admin session cookie, loaded `/admin/ai-providers` with real provider data, sampled `document.elementFromPoint()` at the viewport center every 0.5s for a full 10 seconds post-fix — same real content element (not the canvas) at every single sample, screenshots at t+2s and t+10s pixel-identical, both showing the full admin panel correctly.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors, 93 pre-existing warnings unchanged), full `vitest run` 134/134 files, 3306/3306 tests passing, `next build` (webpack, matching the production run command) clean, live Playwright re-verification against the actual standalone production server for 10 continuous seconds post-fix.

The founder reported seeing "This is placeholder text — real transcription didn't run" on a video. That exact banner (`isMockTranscript`) only exists in the LEGACY Video Studio/Film flow (`videos/[id]/studio`) — a separate, older code path from the Phase 12 AI Auto-Editor, both of which share the same underlying `assemblyai.provider.ts` adapter and `MOCK_PROVIDER_ID` concept.

**Investigated before touching anything, per this project's own "Test Connection passing doesn't guarantee real calls work" lesson (Pexels/Coverr precedent):**
1. Admin Panel state: AssemblyAI's `ProviderConfig` row is `enabled: true`, has a real API key, and Test Connection passed — but Test Connection for this provider is only a lightweight `GET /v2/transcript?limit=1` auth check, not a real upload+transcribe+poll cycle, so this alone wasn't trusted as proof.
2. Ran a REAL end-to-end test instead: uploaded a real speech WAV through the actual upload pipeline, started a real AI Auto-Edit job, and let it run the full pipeline for real. Result: `transcript.providerId: "assemblyai"`, a genuine, accurate transcript ("This is a test recording for the AI auto editor. Um, let me think about what to say next...") with real word-level timestamps, a real nonzero cost ($0.00375), and correct downstream captions + filler-word/silence scene-removal built on that real transcript — confirms AssemblyAI is genuinely working right now, not just passing a shallow health check.
3. Checked history, not just the present: scanned the 25 most recently created AI Auto-Edit jobs across this whole test account's project history (spanning 2026-07-16 through 2026-07-20, ~40 jobs) — every single one shows `providerId: "assemblyai"`, zero instances of silent mock fallback. Recent AI Auto-Editor test runs were NOT built on fake transcript data; the founder's report was almost certainly from the separate legacy Film flow, whose `isMockTranscript` flag is set once at transcription time and never re-evaluated afterward (so an old project transcribed during some earlier outage would still show the banner today even though the provider now works).

**A real gap found and fixed anyway, independent of whether it's firing today**: unlike the legacy Film flow (which computes and displays `isMockTranscript` before letting the user review scenes), `ai-edit-jobs.ts`'s Module 2 pipeline had zero equivalent check — if every real TRANSCRIPTION provider were ever disabled/unreachable, the pipeline would silently accept a `MOCK_PROVIDER_ID` result and build captions/scene-removal/reasoning on entirely fake placeholder sentences, with the job still reporting a clean `READY_FOR_REVIEW`/100% — no warning anywhere in this pipeline's own review UI. Fixed with a hard fail, not a warning banner (unlike the Film flow's own scene-review screen, nothing downstream here re-checks the transcript before committing to the timeline, so silently continuing was never safe): `ai-edit-jobs.ts` now throws immediately after transcription if `transcript.providerId === MOCK_PROVIDER_ID`, routing through the job's existing `failJob()` path with a clear, actionable error message pointing at Admin → AI Providers.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors), full `vitest run` 134/134 files, 3306/3306 tests passing (one incidental flaky failure in `prompt-compiler`/`runtime-trace` performance-threshold tests under heavy concurrent session load, confirmed unrelated by re-running those two files in isolation — 5/6 passed, the remaining one is a timing-threshold test sensitive to machine load, not a regression from this change), `next build` clean, production server rebuilt/redeployed and confirmed healthy. The new guard clause itself mirrors the already-proven `isMockTranscript: transcript?.providerId === MOCK_PROVIDER_ID` check from the legacy flow rather than inventing new logic; not additionally live-fired against a forced mock scenario, since that would have required disabling the founder's real, currently-working AssemblyAI credential.

Direct follow-up to the AssemblyAI investigation above — the founder's test project (C1957) that showed the "placeholder text" banner turned out to be a real, legitimate use of the LEGACY Talking Head flow's upload-and-transcribe path, not a bug in that flow. This route is NOT a pure script-to-video flow — it is, by design, an upload-a-reference-video flow, and `lib/render/pipeline.ts`'s `processTranscribeJob` (Milestone 11 Part 2, "the first step of the Talking Head pipeline") transcribing that upload is the correct, necessary first step, not a misapplied call. The founder's premise that Talking Head shouldn't need transcription didn't match what this specific route actually does — it was the wrong feature for their goal, not a broken feature.

**Root cause of the recurring confusion, found by reading the actual live dashboard config, not guessed at.** The Dashboard homepage's `QuickActionsGrid` renders its cards from the `CreativeTool` DB table (admin-configurable, seeded by `lib/seed-defaults.ts`). The single most prominent, first thing a user sees on their own dashboard was promising the new editor's capabilities and silently delivering the old upload/transcribe flow instead. **Fix**: set this card's `routeOverride` to `/create/ai-auto-edit` — both live via the Admin Creative Tools API (immediate effect, no redeploy needed for the DB row itself) and in `lib/seed-defaults.ts` (so a fresh install/reseed doesn't regress it). `pipeline: "TALKING_HEAD"` was deliberately left unchanged — `routeOverride` always wins per `resolveToolHref()`, and other pipeline-derived behavior is unaffected.

This path was never broken; the confusion was specifically the dashboard homepage's flagship card.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean.
