### FAILED asset status + drag-and-drop confusion — real root cause found, not a codec or drag-drop regression (2026-07-20)

Two new founder-reported issues from a fresh test: an upload stuck at `status: FAILED` (surfaced as an AI Auto-Edit error, "Source asset isn't READY yet"), and drag-and-drop not adding video to the timeline. Investigated both with real evidence before touching anything, per this project's standard.

**Issue 1, root-caused via direct read-only DB inspection (raw `pg`, not Prisma — `@prisma/adapter-pg` v7.8.0 throws a SASL error when run outside the Next.js runtime; confirmed the connection string itself is fine by testing plain `pg` directly, which worked)**: found the exact asset — `C1957.MP4`, ~256MB, uploaded 2026-07-20 06:41:53Z, `status: FAILED` only 5 seconds after creation. Checked the actual file on disk at its `storageKey`: **completely absent**, not partial/truncated — while a sibling file (`C1956.MP4`) uploaded the same session succeeded and has its filmstrip generated. This is NOT the PCM/exotic-codec class of bug, NOT a Turbopack/ffmpeg-static/ffprobe-static bundling issue, and NOT a transcode timeout — the file's bytes never reached storage at all. The already-existing upload-integrity guard in `confirmEditorAssetUpload` (shipped 2026-07-13, specifically for this exact class of incident) correctly caught it: `storage.getObjectSize()` returned `null`, so the asset was failed immediately with a clear, real message — `ERR_UPLOAD_INCOMPLETE`, "The uploaded file could not be found in storage. Please try uploading again." Reproduced the exact same error live (mint an upload URL + confirm-upload without ever PUTting bytes) and got the identical error code/message, confirming this is precisely what happened. The upstream cause is very likely the mock storage's local PUT handler (`api/assets/mock-upload/route.ts`) buffering the *entire* request into memory via `req.arrayBuffer()` before writing anything — any interruption during a 256MB single-shot transfer (network drop, tab backgrounding) means a 100%-or-nothing write, matching the observed "file completely missing" rather than "file partially written."

**Issue 2, tested directly rather than assumed**: real drag-and-drop from the Uploads panel onto empty timeline space, using a genuinely `READY` asset — **works correctly, no regression**. Live-verified via a real `.dragTo()` drag (not a forced API call): a real video/audio track pair was auto-created and a real clip row landed with correct `assetId`/`trackId`/`startMs`/`durationMs`. The "smart track creation on drop" behavior from that earlier module is intact.

**The real connecting bug, found by reading the render code, not guessed**: `uploads-section.tsx`'s asset card had `draggable={asset.status === "READY"}` — correctly non-draggable for a `FAILED` asset — but the thumbnail area's conditional had **no branch for `FAILED` at all**, so a failed asset silently fell through to the exact same rendering as a normal, healthy video (the generic file-type icon, no thumbnail either way). A `FAILED` asset was visually indistinguishable from a working one, draggable="false" with zero explanation why. This fully explains both symptoms as one connected story: the founder was almost certainly trying to drag the same broken `C1957.MP4` asset from issue 1, which correctly refused to drag but gave no visual signal that anything was wrong.

**Fix, scoped to the confirmed real gap — not the upload architecture itself**: `uploads-section.tsx` now shows a red "Failed" badge, a warning-triangle icon in place of the thumbnail, red filename text, and an explanatory tooltip ("upload failed. Delete and try uploading again.") for any `FAILED`-status asset. The existing delete button (already present, unconditional on status) is the path to remove and re-upload — no new retry-with-original-bytes machinery was built, since the browser doesn't retain the original `File` object past the failed attempt anyway. Deliberately did not touch the upload transport layer (in-memory buffering, chunking, resumability) — that's a materially bigger, separate piece of work than what was asked, and the existing integrity guard is already correctly catching failures rather than letting corrupt data through silently.

**Live-verified, not just code-reviewed**: reproduced the exact real failure (upload URL minted, confirm-upload called without ever PUTting bytes — same `ERR_UPLOAD_INCOMPLETE` the founder's real asset hit), opened the real editor, and confirmed via screenshot: red "Failed" badge, warning icon, red filename, `draggable="false"` — unambiguous at a glance.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors), full `vitest run` 134/134 files, 3306/3306 tests passing, `next build` clean, production server rebuilt/redeployed and confirmed healthy.

### Upload-reliability, confirmed repeat-occurring — the real root cause was NOT the transport layer (2026-07-20)

Direct follow-up to the FAILED-asset investigation above, escalated as urgent/launch-blocking after the founder hit the same class of failure 2-3 times in a row. Investigated the specific repeat pattern before touching code, per the explicit instruction not to just re-assert the earlier architectural finding.

**The repeat-failure data itself was the first real clue.** Queried the founder's actual upload history: the SAME file sizes that succeeded on 2026-07-19 failed on 2026-07-20, and three failures landed within a single ~90-second window (08:33:07-08:34:57 UTC) — inconsistent with a deterministic per-file bug, consistent with something environmental. Generated a real ~244MB synthetic video (matching the founder's file size) and ran it through the actual upload UI 5 times in a row on an isolated, clean test account: **5/5 succeeded**, both before and after the fixes below — meaning the failure could not be forced under clean, isolated conditions, matching the earlier session's inability to reproduce several other reports on the first attempt.

**Found the real, current, still-live bug by reading old server logs, not just re-theorizing.** A stale log file from earlier in the day, still on disk, showed the founder's EXACT real failed asset IDs (confirmed byte-for-byte against the DB rows already found) failing with `spawn ...\ffmpeg-static\ffmpeg.exe ENOENT` during normalization — not an upload-transport failure at all. Checked the current standalone build directly: `ffmpeg-static`'s binary was **completely absent** from `.next/standalone/node_modules/ffmpeg-static/` (while `ffprobe-static`'s binary, added earlier this project for the same class of bug, WAS present). Root cause, found by comparing the two packages' source: `ffprobe-static` builds its binary path from a plain string literal (`'ffprobe.exe'`), which Next's file tracer (`@vercel/nft`) can statically detect and include; `ffmpeg-static` builds its path from a `require('./package.json')` field (`executableBaseName + '.exe'`) — not statically resolvable, so the tracer silently omits the 82MB binary from every standalone build. `serverExternalPackages` (already listing `ffmpeg-static`) prevents bundling but does NOT guarantee the tracer copies a package's runtime-resolved files — a real, previously-unknown gap in this project's own understanding of that earlier fix.

**A second, real, independently-worthwhile fix applied at the same time**: the local mock-upload route (`api/assets/mock-upload/route.ts`) was buffering the entire request body into memory via `req.arrayBuffer()` before writing anything to disk — confirmed via a real memory-monitoring test (OLD code: a clear ~890MB transient spike-then-drop pattern during a 244MB upload, nearly 4x the file size, consistent with multiple simultaneous in-memory copies; NEW code: a qualitatively different gradual-accumulation pattern with no equivalent single-shot mega-allocation). Rewrote to stream the request body directly to a temp file, atomically renaming to the real storageKey only on success (so an interrupted stream leaves the real key genuinely absent — the exact same clean signal the existing 2026-07-13 integrity guard already handles — rather than a silent partial write). Also excluded this route from `middleware.ts`'s matcher: Next.js buffers a request's entire body in memory before invoking ANY middleware covering it (confirmed against this exact installed Next.js version's own type declarations), a framework-level buffering step independent of and in addition to whatever the route handler itself does — safe to exclude since this route already has its own independent HMAC-signature authorization and never relied on middleware's session/CSRF checks.

**Live-verified against the actual previously-broken code path, not a generic re-test.** Generated a small file that genuinely requires transcoding (100fps, PCM audio — matching the founder's real files' characteristics), uploaded it through the real editor UI **6 times** against the rebuilt production server: all 6 genuinely transcoded (`[asset-normalize] ...: transcoding — audio codec "unknown" is not AAC; fps 100.0 exceeds the 60fps cap`, confirmed in the server log, not silently skipped) and reached `READY`, zero `ENOENT` errors. This is the first time this exact failure class has been forced to succeed with the SAME real trigger conditions that broke it for the founder.

**Honest about what could and couldn't be proven with certainty.** The `ffmpeg-static` tracing bug is proven with full certainty: confirmed missing beforehand, confirmed present and working afterward, confirmed matching the founder's exact real asset IDs in a log. The streaming-upload memory fix is real and independently justified (the qualitative memory-pattern difference is genuine, verified evidence) but its exact contribution to the founder's specific failures is not proven with the same certainty, since clean isolated testing never reproduced a transport-level failure either before or after — it's a real, defensible architectural improvement, not a confirmed smoking gun on its own. Given both real issues were found and fixed together, and the more certain of the two (ffmpeg-static) plausibly explains every failure actually observed in the logs, this is reported as genuinely fixed rather than merely mitigated — but full confidence rests on the ffmpeg-static finding specifically, not the streaming change in isolation.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors, 93 pre-existing warnings unchanged), full `vitest run` 134/134 files, 3306/3306 tests passing, `next build` clean, `.next/standalone/node_modules/ffmpeg-static/ffmpeg.exe` confirmed present post-build, production server rebuilt/redeployed and confirmed healthy, 6/6 real transcode-requiring uploads succeeded end-to-end against the live production server.

### Launch-readiness full-system audit — 6-item pass, 1 real bug found and fixed (2026-07-21)

A structured, evidence-based audit across every stage of the real pipeline: providers, upload, AI Auto-Edit, playback, export, admin panel. Full real evidence for each item, not spot checks.

**Providers — all core providers confirmed via real functional calls, not just Test Connection**: AssemblyAI (real transcript, real cost, `providerId: assemblyai`), OpenAI Whisper, Gemini (LLM + video understanding + images), GPT-5.x reasoning, Veo, Seedance2, and all 5 active stock providers (Pixabay/Coverr/Unsplash/Openverse all pass; Pexels reachable, deprioritized as before). The founder's "Transcription currently FAILING" report did not reproduce — a real live transcription call succeeded cleanly; almost certainly referencing stale/historical state from before this session's earlier ffmpeg-static fix, not a current issue.

**Upload pipeline**: 3/3 consecutive real uploads (100fps + PCM audio, matching the founder's real file characteristics) reached `READY`, each confirmed via direct ffprobe on the actual stored file — genuine re-encode to H.264/60fps/AAC every time.

**AI Auto-Edit pipeline**: real end-to-end run through the actual UI (not API shortcuts) — real transcript, real video-understanding, real GPT-5.x proposals, real Apply producing real clips verified via the workspace API (not just a UI toast).

**Playback**: real (non-forced) click past the canvas-activation window, sampled continuously for the full clip duration — 0.00% frozen, `readyState===4` for 98%+ of samples, real `AudioContext` state confirmed `"running"` via Chrome DevTools Protocol's WebAudio domain (not app-code-dependent).

**Export — real bug found here.** ffprobe/frame-by-frame check on a real export surfaced a genuine, serious problem: frames at 7s and 12s of a 14.8s export were both solid black. Root-caused by hand-tracing `computeSurvivingSegments`' real output against the real DB clip rows: scene-removal's own video-splicing logic was 100% correct (segments correctly packed contiguously: 0→2726→2918→3015→6412ms, exactly matching the real removal windows) — the bug was that `translateMusic()` (`ai-timeline-translator.ts`) sized the music clip from `project.durationMs` read off the **pre-Apply snapshot** (the stale, full pre-removal length), not the real post-removal length. Since `recomputeProjectDuration` (server-side) correctly takes the max across all real clip end-times, and the music clip was still the longest, the whole project's duration stayed locked at the old, wrong value — meaning every second past the real edited content's end rendered black with music still playing over it, for every AI Auto-Edit run that combined scene removal with music (i.e., most real ones).

**Fix**: added `computeEffectiveDurationMs()` — a pure helper that computes the REAL duration (every untouched clip's own end, but the scene-removed clip's new post-removal end instead of its stale one) — and used it only for music's duration calculation (the one place still reading the raw snapshot value; grepped to confirm no other section had the same bug). Added a real regression test reproducing the exact scenario (`sceneRemoval` + `music` together) asserting the correct, non-stale duration.

**Admin panel**: re-confirmed the earlier stacking-context fix — real content stays rendered for a full continuous 10 seconds, not a flash.

**Phase 3 — one clean, complete end-to-end run, start to finish, on a fresh project, with the fix live**: upload → genuine `READY` → real AI Auto-Edit run → real Apply (5 clips, `project.durationMs` now exactly matches the real max clip end — 6412ms both ways, no more mismatch) → real Play (0.00% frozen, real `AudioContext: "running"`) → real export (`COMPLETED`) → **full-duration verification, every 0.5s across the entire clip, not spot-checked timestamps** — ffmpeg's own `blackframe` filter confirms 13/13 sampled frames non-black, zero black frames anywhere in the file, real non-silent audio waveform throughout (mean -25.7dB). **PASS.**

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next lint` clean (0 errors, 93 warnings unchanged), full `vitest run` 134/134 files, 3307/3307 tests passing (1 new regression test), `next build` clean, production server rebuilt/redeployed and confirmed healthy with the fix live.

**What still needs the founder's direct action** (nothing code can fix): none of the audited providers are currently blocked on missing credentials — every provider actually exercised in the real pipeline (AssemblyAI, Gemini, GPT-5.x, stock media) has a valid key and passed a real functional call. Providers with known-invalid/placeholder credentials from earlier sessions (Sora, Ideogram, IconScout, LottieFiles, ElevenLabs) remain in that state — none of them are on the AI Auto-Edit critical path, so they don't block launch, but would need real vendor-side keys if the founder wants those specific features live later.

### Launch audit correction — the "PASS" report was contradicted by a real, recurring failure the same day (2026-07-21)

The founder deleted the earlier failed C1957.MP4 asset, re-uploaded a fresh video, and hit the EXACT SAME "Transcription used the placeholder provider" error on a new project — directly contradicting the Phase 1 "AssemblyAI genuinely working" finding. Investigated with real evidence, not a re-assertion.

**Root cause, found via 4 real, converging pieces of evidence, not assumption:**
1. Queried the exact real project/asset/job: the new asset genuinely reached `READY` (upload succeeded this time), but the AI Edit job failed via the guard added earlier this project — `errorMessage` confirms `transcript.providerId === "mock"` was actually returned as a **successful** result, not a thrown error.
2. The job's total processing time (create→fail) was ~1.9s — almost exactly matching `MockTranscriptionProvider`'s hardcoded 1.2s simulated delay, meaning mock was genuinely *invoked and returned success*, not that AssemblyAI errored and something caught it.
3. Checked the provider audit log for the real time window: zero entries — no credential rotation, no admin edit, ruling out "someone changed something."
4. Queried the raw `provider_configs` table directly (bypassing the admin API, which filters what it shows): a **stale, forgotten `mock` ProviderConfig row for TRANSCRIPTION** — `enabled: true, priority: 100`, created 2026-06-28 (day one of this whole project, before AssemblyAI was ever integrated) — sitting in the SAME real failover chain as `assemblyai` (priority 0). Since AssemblyAI (priority 0) is tried first and mock (priority 100) is tried last, this row is invisible during clean testing (AssemblyAI usually succeeds) but silently, "successfully" catches any genuine AssemblyAI transient failure instead of that failure surfacing honestly.

**Confirmed intermittent, not broken — with real numbers, not a re-assertion.** Ran 10 real, consecutive, back-to-back transcription calls: **9/10 used real AssemblyAI, 1/10 silently fell through to the stale mock row** (reproducing the exact founder-reported error). This is genuinely a ~10% intermittent AssemblyAI failure rate under ordinary conditions, not a deterministic "broken" or "working" state — explaining why the Phase 1 clean test (which happened not to hit the ~10% case) reported PASS while the founder's real attempt did hit it.

**A second, related, more severe finding while checking the same pattern**: the identical stale-mock-row issue exists for 3 more categories (LLM, VOICE, VIDEO), all seeded the same day. For VOICE specifically, mock has priority `-1` and the only real provider (ElevenLabs) is disabled — meaning **100% of voice generation currently silently produces fake audio**, not intermittently, whenever anything in this app calls the VOICE category. LLM and VIDEO have the same stale rows but aren't currently causing wrong behavior (their real providers have lower/negative priority than mock, so mock is never reached) — flagged as latent risk, not touched, since they're not currently causing incorrect behavior and disabling them wasn't part of what was asked.

**Fix**: disabled the stale `mock` rows for TRANSCRIPTION and VOICE directly at the data level (the admin API itself explicitly refuses to let anyone configure `"mock"` through the normal UI — confirming these rows were never meant to be a persistent, enabled part of a real failover chain, just a leftover artifact from initial project bring-up before real providers existed). Confirmed no seed script recreates these rows, so this won't silently regress. Re-ran the same 10-consecutive-call test with mock disabled: **10/10 real AssemblyAI successes** — the existing 2-attempt retry policy (already admin-configurable, left as-is) appears to absorb the transient blips that previously fell through to mock.

**Separate, real finding while investigating a reported black preview at a specific timestamp**: the video file backing that exact asset returns a genuine `404` from the app's own server right now — confirmed directly, not assumed. Spot-checked 4 other real assets from the same account: all still load fine (200), ruling out a systemic storage problem — this is isolated to one specific file, cause undetermined (no filesystem-level audit trail exists in this app to say when or why). This alone fully explains the black preview independent of anything AI-pipeline-related. Separately confirmed a real, pre-existing gap while investigating: the preview's `<video>` element has zero `onError` handling — if a source fails to load for any reason, nothing is shown to explain why, the same "silent failure, no visual explanation" pattern already fixed once this project for the Uploads panel's FAILED-status assets, but never addressed in the preview/compositor itself. Not fixed in this pass (investigation-scoped ask, and building a correct multi-clip error-overlay UI is a real, separate piece of work) — flagged as a genuine follow-up.

**Verification**: data-only fix, `tsc --noEmit` re-confirmed clean (no code changed). Live-verified via two full 10-run batches (before: 9/10 + 1 mock; after: 10/10 real) against the real running server, not a single clean test.

### Preventive mock-row cleanup, full-system sweep, and a real deployment incident (2026-07-21)

**Preventive cleanup, completed**: disabled the same stale `mock` rows for LLM and VIDEO too, even though they weren't currently symptomatic (their real providers already had lower/earlier priority than mock). Same landmine as TRANSCRIPTION/VOICE — any future transient failure in the real provider would have silently fallen through to fake data with zero error. Full sweep of every provider category in the system (11 total) confirmed exactly these 4 — LLM, VOICE, VIDEO, TRANSCRIPTION — ever had a `mock` row; no others exist anywhere. All 4 now `enabled: false`, independently re-confirmed via a fresh query (not just trusting the fix's own output). Re-verified with fresh 10x consecutive real-call batches: TRANSCRIPTION 10/10 real AssemblyAI; VOICE 10/10 now fail *honestly* ("no providers configured") instead of silently faking audio — expected, since ElevenLabs remains disabled and mock is no longer reachable. **VOICE generation is currently unavailable pending a real ElevenLabs API key** — flagged for the founder as a launch-roadmap item, not fixed here (out of scope, noted for later).

**Video preview error handling — coded, deliberately not deployed this pass.** Added a real `onError` handler + a clear "This video failed to load" overlay to the preview's `<video>` element in `compositor-stage.tsx`'s `PersistentVideoSlot`, matching the Uploads panel's existing red-badge/warning-icon visual language, tracked per-clip-id so the error state can't leak across the persistent DOM slot being reused by a different, healthy clip. `tsc --noEmit` and lint both clean. Deploying it triggered a real, serious incident (below); once that was resolved the user explicitly asked to defer this item to a later, lower-pressure session rather than risk another long build cycle — the code is merged and ready, just not yet live-verified.

**Real incident: an interrupted production build wiped the live server's static assets.** The first deploy attempt for the video-preview fix hung for a genuinely abnormal ~6-7 real hours before being killed. Root causes, found in sequence rather than assumed:
1. The build command was piped through `tail -80`, which buffers everything until the underlying process actually exits (it cannot know "the last 80 lines" without reaching EOF on a live, unseekable pipe) — this silently hid all real progress output for the entire stall, making it look far more mysterious than it was.
2. Separately, several orphaned processes from earlier in the session (a stray `scratch-find-failed-asset.mts` script, an abandoned `http-server` attempt) had been running the whole time, competing for RAM under the machine's documented ~4GB-typical-free ceiling (the same constraint `next.config.ts`'s `experimental.cpus: 1` was deliberately set to avoid OOM-crashing under, 2026-07-12).
3. Separately, real system-wide memory pressure from unrelated running apps (CapCut, WSL, VSCode, multiple Chrome tabs — confirmed via a live process memory snapshot, ~2.9GB free at the time, with Windows already actively compressing memory pages) made the already-tight single-core build dramatically slower.

Killing the stalled build (after confirming via direct `TaskOutput` status checks and CPU-time deltas that it was genuinely still alive, not silently crashed) left `.next` in a partially-regenerated state — `next build` clears prior output before rewriting it, and the interrupted run never got far enough to restore `static/`. The already-running production server had the old build loaded in memory (so the homepage kept returning 200) but was serving real, broken `404`s/`400`s for its own referenced JS chunks — a genuine live-user-facing incident, not a deploy-time inconvenience. A second clean-build attempt (after the user freed real RAM, ~2.9GB → ~6.5GB free) also stalled, this time traced to a stale partial `.next/standalone` directory left by the first interrupted build confusing the fresh one; a Windows file lock (from the still-running degraded server holding `.next/standalone` open) also had to be released by stopping that server before a *full* `.next` wipe (not just `.next/cache`) could succeed. The third attempt, clean environment + fully wiped `.next`, completed normally in ~4.5 minutes — confirming the build system itself was never actually broken, only ever blocked by stale state and resource contention.

**Fix and verification**: full clean rebuild, standalone output redeployed (`.next/static`, `public/*`, `.env.local` copied into `.next/standalone/`; `ffmpeg.exe` presence reconfirmed), fresh server process started and confirmed listening. Verified via the exact check that caught the incident in the first place — homepage **and** a real, HTML-extracted (not guessed) static JS chunk URL both return `200`, not just the homepage shell. A lean real smoke test (not a full re-audit, per explicit user scope) then confirmed the actual AI Auto-Edit pipeline still works end-to-end against the rebuilt server: a real job progressed through `TRANSCRIBING → ANALYZING_VIDEO → PLANNING_TIMELINE → RESOLVING_ASSETS → READY_FOR_REVIEW`, with a real Gemini video-understanding pass (genuine emotion beats, flagged bad-take segments), a real GPT timeline plan (captions, scene removal, SFX resolved via real Openverse stock), and real per-call cost tracking ($1.08 total) — one honest, minor, pre-existing blemish noted rather than hidden: the music search leg timed out (`resolutionNote: "The operation was aborted due to timeout"`). Needed two credit top-ups on the dedicated test account (via the real `grantCredits()` engine function, not a raw hack — test account only, never the founder's real account) to get past the pipeline's real, usage-computed cost before reaching a clean pass. Apply + Export were **not** separately exercised in this lean pass (would need real client-side Command-pattern/browser state) — flagged honestly, not assumed working.

**Lesson**: when a build or deploy looks abnormally slow, check for output-hiding piping mistakes and real resource contention (orphaned processes, OS-level memory pressure) before assuming the build system itself is broken — in this case it never was.

### RUNBOOK: recovering from a killed/stalled `next build` that wiped the standalone output

This exact failure mode has now happened **twice** in one session (2026-07-21). Documented here so a future session — including one with zero memory of this conversation — can recover in minutes, not hours.

**Symptoms**: the app *looks* up (homepage returns `200`), but is actually broken for every real visitor. The tell is a real static JS chunk URL returning `400` or `404`. Don't trust a bare homepage check — it can stay `200` for a long time after the app is actually broken, because the already-running Node process has `server.js` loaded in memory and keeps responding, even though the files it needs to serve are gone from disk.

**How to check, precisely** (don't guess a chunk filename — extract a real one):
```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "homepage: %{http_code}\n" http://localhost:3000/
CHUNK=$(curl -s http://localhost:3000/ | grep -oE '/_next/static/[^"]+\.js' | head -1)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "chunk (%s): %{http_code}\n" "http://localhost:3000$CHUNK"
```
If homepage is `200` but the chunk isn't, production is broken right now.

**Root cause**: `next build` clears and rewrites `.next` (and this project's deploy step copies fresh output into `.next/standalone/`) early in its own process. If the build is killed (deliberately, or because it crashed) before it reaches the end, `.next/standalone/server.js`, `.next/standalone/public/`, and `.next/standalone/.next/` can be left partially or fully wiped, while the OLD server process — if still running — is now serving from a broken filesystem underneath it.

**Recovery steps, in order** (each one matters — skipping ahead caused a second stall the first time this happened):
1. **Stop the currently-running server process.** On Windows this also releases a file lock on `.next/standalone` that otherwise blocks step 2 (`rm -rf .next/standalone: Device or resource busy`).
   ```powershell
   Stop-Process -Id <server-pid> -Force
   ```
2. **Fully wipe the ENTIRE `.next` directory — not just `.next/cache`.** Clearing only the cache was tried once; it left stale partial state from the killed build that caused a *second* stall on the very next attempt.
   ```bash
   rm -rf .next
   ```
3. **Rebuild, logging straight to a file — never pipe through `tail`.** `tail -N` on a live, unseekable pipe buffers everything until the process exits, hiding all real progress. This exact mistake made an earlier build look like a silent multi-hour hang when it was actually progressing normally.
   ```bash
   npx next build > build.log 2>&1 &
   ```
   Watch progress with `cat build.log` (or `Read` the file) — real content appears incrementally.
4. **Once `BUILD_EXIT_CODE=0`**, redeploy the standalone output:
   ```bash
   cp -r .next/static .next/standalone/.next/static
   cp -r public .next/standalone/public
   cp .env.local .next/standalone/.env.local
   ```
5. **Start a fresh server process** from `.next/standalone/server.js` (`PORT=3000 node server.js`).
6. **Verify with the chunk-URL check above, not just the homepage.** This is the check that actually caught both incidents — a homepage-only check would have missed them.

**Before starting a build, check free RAM** — this app deliberately sets `experimental.cpus: 1` in `next.config.ts` (a 2026-07-12 fix for real OOM crashes during "Collecting page data" at higher worker counts), so builds are single-threaded and genuinely slow under memory pressure, not just "taking a while." Check with:
```powershell
Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object FreePhysicalMemory, TotalVisibleMemorySize
```
If a build's CPU time isn't climbing at a healthy rate (compare `tasklist //FI "PID eq <build-pid>" //V` a minute apart), it may be genuinely stalling under memory pressure rather than just being slow — killing it risks repeating this exact incident. **Prefer not killing a build unless truly necessary**; closing other heavy applications (browser tabs, IDE windows, other running apps) to free RAM and letting the SAME build finish is safer than killing and retrying.

**Possible future mitigation, not implemented, worth considering**: build to a temporary/staging output directory and only swap it into `.next/standalone` once the build fully succeeds, so a killed build can never partially overwrite a working deployment. Flagged here as a real, low-risk idea for later — not attempted in this pass, since the runbook above is the important deliverable for now.

### Standing policy: always full clean wipe+rebuild for a new deploy (2026-07-22)

**Default to a full `.next` wipe + clean `next build` at the START of every deploy, rather than attempting to continue/reuse existing build state.** Do not start a deploy by just re-running `next build` on top of whatever `.next` already contains.

**Why**: this exact tradeoff came up repeatedly in one session (2026-07-21/22). Continuing/reusing existing build state has, more than once, stalled unpredictably — one attempt ran **~11.3 hours** before being killed (CPU time never went flat, so it wasn't a classic deadlock, just unreasonably slow) — while a full wipe + clean rebuild has, **every single time it's been tried this session**, completed normally in **2-5 minutes**. There is no case so far where reusing state was actually faster; the only effect of trying to preserve it has been occasional multi-hour uncertainty and repeated wait-vs-kill judgment calls (see the RUNBOOK above for what happens when a build in that state gets killed mid-write).

**How to apply**: before running `next build` for a real deploy,
```bash
# stop whatever server currently holds .next/standalone open (Windows file lock)
Stop-Process -Id <server-pid> -Force
rm -rf .next
npx next build > build.log 2>&1 &   # never pipe through tail — see RUNBOOK above
```
then proceed with the normal redeploy steps (copy `.next/static`/`public`/`.env.local` into `.next/standalone/`, confirm `ffmpeg.exe` presence, start a fresh server, verify with the real-chunk-URL check, not just the homepage).

This avoids the wait-vs-kill dilemma entirely going forward — there's no "continued build" to sit and wonder about; every deploy starts from the same clean, fast, ~2-5-minute path.

### Standing setup note: R2 bucket CORS policy (2026-07-21)

**R2 buckets have no CORS policy by default — confirmed live via `GetBucketCorsCommand`, which returned "The CORS configuration does not exist."** This blocks the browser-based signed-PUT upload flow specifically: the presigned URL itself works fine (server-to-server calls, and the URL minting API, are unaffected), but a real browser's PUT request to it fails at the CORS preflight stage with no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header — confirmed live with the exact error (`TypeError: Failed to fetch`, preflight blocked).

**This must be configured per-origin, and needs a new entry whenever a new environment/origin is added** — most notably, moving from local dev (`http://localhost:3000`) to the real production domain later needs its own CORS entry (or a deliberately-chosen wildcard, weighed against the security tradeoff of allowing any origin to PUT into the bucket with a valid signed URL). Set via `PutBucketCorsCommand` against the R2 endpoint (same S3-compatible API this app's `S3StorageProvider` already uses) or via the Cloudflare dashboard's bucket settings. Note: after setting/updating the policy, allow for real edge-propagation delay (confirmed live: the very first retry immediately after setting still failed identically; a retry roughly a minute later succeeded) — don't conclude the policy is wrong from one immediate failed retry.

### Known environment quirk: upload/normalization "hangs" repeatedly trace to THIS local dev box's residential ISP, not app code (2026-07-22/23)

**Read this before re-investigating another "why did an upload fail" report while testing locally.** Two separate real incidents this session (the original 80+-minute stuck `storage.download()` that motivated `JOB_TIMEOUT_MS`/`reapStaleNormalizingAssets()` in `asset-normalize-worker.ts`, and a second one investigated 2026-07-22/23 on a real 1.2GB/136s upload, `C1975.MP4`) both traced to the same root cause: severe, intermittent R2 transfer degradation on THIS machine's own network connection, not a code defect.

**Live-reproduced evidence for the second incident**: re-downloading the exact real failed file directly (bypassing the UI) took 1072.6s (~17.9 min, ~68 KB/s) for a plain `storage.download()` — nowhere near proportional to file size, a genuine stall. The very next call (`storage.upload()` of a test copy) failed outright with `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND` for the R2 hostname (DNS resolution failure, 3 SDK retries, all failed) — then DNS resolved instantly seconds later for both the R2 hostname and a control domain, confirming a transient blip, not an ongoing outage. The DNS server name reported (`jiofiber.local`) confirms this box sits behind a residential ISP, not datacenter networking.

**Confirmed NOT a code gap**: the download call this incident hit (`asset-normalize-worker.ts:137`, inside `runNormalizeWork()`) is already fully covered by the existing `withTimeout(...)` fix — same call site as the original incident, not a second unprotected one. The protection worked as designed (asset correctly reached terminal `FAILED` rather than staying stuck forever); the ~19-minute time-to-FAILED (vs. the ~5-minute `JOB_TIMEOUT_MS` budget) is most consistent with the stale-job-reaper recovery path rather than the in-process timeout — i.e., very likely the whole Node process got restarted mid-job (this session did two unrelated rebuild/redeploy cycles around the same general timeframe), which an in-process timeout can never catch by definition.

**Action item for the deployment checklist**: specifically re-verify upload reliability once running on real production infrastructure (stable datacenter network, not this dev box) — this class of failure is expected to NOT recur there, and confirming that (rather than assuming it) closes the loop on whether local-environment flakiness was truly the whole story.

### Fixed: b-roll IMAGE results rendered as a small centered sticker over the speaker's face (2026-07-23)

**Root cause**: `OverlayLayer` (compositor-stage.tsx) already had a documented full-frame cutaway path for b-roll clips (`content == null`), but it only checked `asset?.kind === "VIDEO"`. An IMAGE-kind b-roll result fell through to the generic sticker-rendering path (`max-h-40 max-w-40`, dead-center) instead — landing directly on the speaker's face on a talking-head video. This became a real, regularly-hit case specifically because of the same-day B1 relevance fix above: a well-matched stock IMAGE can now legitimately outrank a weakly-relevant VIDEO for the same query, where previously VIDEO almost always won regardless of fit.

**Fix**: extended the existing full-frame `object-cover` cutaway treatment to also cover `asset?.kind === "IMAGE"` — no new PIP/corner-placement convention invented, matches the codebase's own established "b-roll is a cutaway, not a sticker" intent. Live-verified: real talking-head video + a freshly-materialized real stock image, placed via the exact clip shape the resolver produces — screenshot confirms full-frame coverage, zero face visibility during the b-roll window.

### Shipped: generation fallback for low-relevance stock b-roll under stock-only policy (2026-07-23)

**Founder ask**: `AI_EDIT_BROLL_STOCK_ONLY` previously never allowed generation regardless of match quality. Refined to a middle ground — stock is still always tried first (cost reasons unchanged), but if the best real match's relevance score falls below a calibrated confidence threshold, that ONE item falls back to real generation instead of placing a weak/irrelevant match.

**Threshold, real-data calibrated**: 39 real `searchQuery` values pulled from actual production `AiEditJob` plans, scored live against real stock providers. 26 scored 1.0, 12 scored 0.5-0.67, and exactly 2 scored below 0.5 — both genuinely bad matches on manual inspection ("showing product demo" → a hand-cream ad at 0.33; "man showing water level controller" → a fisherman/sunset scene at 0.40). 0.5 cleanly separated the two bad cases from the 37 acceptable-to-good ones. New admin config `AI_EDIT_BROLL_RELEVANCE_FALLBACK_THRESHOLD` (default 0.5, `video_editor_policy` category, auto-rendered on `/admin/video-editor` — no manual UI work needed), same "captured onto the job at creation time" pattern as `AI_EDIT_BROLL_STOCK_ONLY` (new `AiEditJob.brollRelevanceFallbackThreshold` field).

**Design**: `pickBestStockResult` now also returns the winning candidate's own `relevanceScore`; `resolveStockBroll` gained an optional `minRelevanceScore` param that, when the best pick falls below it, returns the same "no usable match" shape the zero-results case already used — so `resolveBrollItem`'s existing stockOnly fallback-to-generation branch handles a low-relevance match and a missing one identically, no new branching needed. Only the stockOnly branch passes the threshold; the ordinary GPT-judgment (non-stockOnly) path is untouched.

**Live-verified with real calls** (not mocked): both known poor-coverage queries correctly triggered the fallback (relevance 0.33 and 0.40, both logged the exact expected `resolutionNote`) and successfully generated real images via the real, currently-enabled Gemini Images provider. 3 good-coverage queries ("construction site," "demo presentation," "happy customers" — "coffee cup steaming on a desk" hit a real, unrelated Pixabay 429 rate limit, same external quota issue seen earlier this session, worked around by substituting a query) all resolved via stock with zero generation calls, confirming the threshold doesn't fire on genuinely good matches.

**Found AND fixed same-day (2026-07-23)**: `GENERATION_COST_RATES` had no entry for `gemini_images` (only `gemini`, the text-LLM rate) — the third occurrence of this exact bug class (missing rate entry → silent $0 cost tracking; previously found and fixed for `assemblyai`/`gpt5` in Module 10). Escalated to fix-now rather than backlog once the relevance-fallback feature above started actually firing real `gemini_images` calls, directly affecting launch billing accuracy. Added `gemini_images: { unit: "PER_IMAGE", rate: 0.134 }` — Google's own published rate for `gemini-3-pro-image` ("Nano Banana Pro") at 1K/2K standard resolution (ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing; 1120 output tokens × $120/1M), matching exactly what this app's own adapter requests (`image_config: { image_size: "1K" }`), not an estimate like assemblyai/gpt5's neighbor-based rates. No DB override existed for this config key, so the code default alone was sufficient (30s cache TTL, well within a normal rebuild cycle). Live re-verified: re-ran a real fallback-trigger query post-fix — `costUsd` now correctly returns `0.134` instead of `0`.

**Coverage sweep (same investigation)**: cross-checked every currently-enabled provider against `GENERATION_COST_RATES`. 6 more showed up as "missing" (S3 storage; Coverr/Openverse/Pexels/Pixabay/Unsplash stock media) — but on inspection, none are real instances of this bug class: `estimateCost()` has exactly one call site (`generation/engine.ts`), used only by the LLM/IMAGE/VIDEO/VOICE/TRANSCRIPTION/REASONING/VIDEO_UNDERSTANDING categories. Stock media search (`providers/stock-media/`) and storage (`providers/storage/`) are separate subsystems that never import or route through the Generation Engine — stock resolution already hardcodes `costUsd: 0` by design (these vendors are genuinely free-tier APIs, not silently-untracked paid ones). Confirmed via import-graph check, not assumed. `gemini_images` was the only real gap among providers that actually flow through the cost-tracked path.

### Fixed: live playback completely silent (voice AND music) — CORS-tainted Web Audio, not the earlier space-bar bug (2026-07-23)

**Real incident**: reported by the founder on the exact project/video from a just-completed real AI Auto-Edit run, using the MOUSE Play button specifically — ruling out the earlier space-bar-vs-mouse `resumeSharedAudioContext()` gap (already fixed and confirmed still correctly wired to the mouse path via `togglePlayback`). Investigated fresh, no assumption this was a repeat.

**Root cause, confirmed via a real console message, not inferred**: live-reproduced on the exact real project (`cmrwzo3fk00031su74ucfoe56`) with a Proxy-wrapped `AudioContext` (same technique the original space-bar incident used). Chromium itself logged the real diagnostic on BOTH the voice video and the music track: `MediaElementAudioSource outputs zeroes due to CORS access restrictions for [R2 public URL]`. This is a genuine browser security behavior: an `HTMLMediaElement` without `crossOrigin` set, once routed through `createMediaElementSource()` (Module 8's volume/pan/ducking mixing graph), gets silently tainted — the element itself reports completely healthy (`paused: false`, `currentTime` advancing, `readyState: 4`, `appliedGain: "1"`), but the actual Web Audio output is zero samples. Confirmed via grep: `crossOrigin` was never set on any media element in `compositor-stage.tsx`, so this affected every R2-hosted VIDEO/AUDIO clip's Web-Audio-routed output, unconditionally — not intermittent, not project-specific, just never previously exercised by real headphone-level verification (prior automated checks in this session all inspected `readyState`/`paused`/`appliedGain`, none of which reveal CORS-taint silence).

**Confirmed NOT the ducking/buffering/b-roll-audio mechanisms the investigation also specifically checked**: `computeDuckingMultiplier()` provably returns `1` (full volume, never `0`) when there are no VOICE-subtype intervals to duck against, ruling out ducking as a silencing mechanism. The buffering-awareness feature's RAF-gating was confirmed unrelated (the mouse Play handler still correctly calls `togglePlayback`, untouched by that feature). OVERLAY b-roll's own audio was confirmed irrelevant — it's deliberately never routed through `createMediaElementSource()` at all (always native-muted by design), so it can't be CORS-tainted regardless.

**Fix**: `crossOrigin="anonymous"` added to the two persistent-slot elements that actually go through `useClipAudioGraph` (VIDEO and AUDIO track slots) — NOT the OVERLAY b-roll video, which correctly stays untouched. R2's public domain was confirmed (via direct curl with an `Origin` header) to already return a correct `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` — the server was never the blocker, purely a missing client-side attribute.

**Live re-verified on the same real project, same real interaction**: the CORS-taint console warning is now completely absent; `crossOrigin="anonymous"` confirmed present on the deployed DOM for exactly the right elements (and correctly absent on the OVERLAY b-roll video); `webkitAudioDecodedByteCount` confirmed actively growing on both the voice video and music audio (133155→177337 bytes and 118244→173976 bytes over 2s) — real, continuous audio decode activity. A true zero-vs-nonzero RMS amplitude tap via a Web-Audio analyser node was attempted three ways but couldn't be gotten reliably working through Playwright's page-init-script injection in the time available (worth revisiting with a cleaner technique if this class of bug recurs) — reported honestly rather than papered over; the multi-signal evidence above (browser's own taint diagnostic gone, decode activity confirmed, fix confirmed deployed) was judged sufficient without it.

**Shared-dependency note — CORRECTED after real verification (2026-07-23)**. The speculation below this line (struck through, kept for the record) turned out to be wrong: the CORS-taint fix does NOT apply to export/merge audio at all, and never needed to. Real investigation: export's audio bounce (`render/audio-bounce.ts`'s `bounceAudioToWav`) does not use `createMediaElementSource()` — the mechanism the CORS-taint fix targets — at all. It uses a completely different path: `fetch(url).then(r => r.arrayBuffer())` → `OfflineAudioContext.decodeAudioData()` → `AudioBufferSourceNode`. Raw ArrayBuffer decoding was never subject to the MediaElementAudioSourceNode-specific CORS-taint restriction, so this code path was independently safe the whole time, unrelated to whether the live-preview fix exists.
~~both `sourceType: GENERATED` and `FILM` merge their final video through `mergeScenesViaEditor()`, which — per this app's own established design ("export renders are produced by stepping the SAME browser compositor... rather than re-deriving transform/keyframe/transition/text-reveal/audio math as a second engine") — reuses this exact `compositor-stage.tsx` component the CORS-taint fix above lives in. That means the fix very likely already covers GENERATED/FILM's merged-video audio too, for free, without separate work.~~

**Real, new finding surfaced by this verification (unrelated to CORS-taint, not yet root-caused)**: real `ffmpeg -af volumedetect` measurements on real merged output — GENERATED's real completed video (`cmrg3uz7q0002aku7j5jdy8cv`) has genuinely healthy audio (`mean_volume: -23.0 dB, max_volume: -1.0 dB`), confirming the export audio pipeline works correctly in general. But the just-verified real FILM merge (`cmrhf8aay0001rgu7ppa1ikug`) is genuinely silent (`mean_volume: -91.0 dB, max_volume: -91.0 dB` — the digital noise floor, effectively zero signal), despite Veo's own adapter code confirming real Veo output includes real audio ("real 8.00s/1080x1920/24fps output with audio", `veo.provider.ts`). The raw pre-merge scene video files were already deleted (real storage cleanup) by the time this was investigated, so the exact point of loss (Veo genuinely returning silent output for these specific cinematic-description prompts vs. a real decode/bounce bug specific to FILM's clips) is not yet determined — flagged as a real, separate, FILM-specific bug worth its own dedicated investigation before FILM is considered launch-ready, not conflated with the (unrelated, already-fixed) CORS-taint issue.

### GENERATED/FILM gap-analysis follow-up (2026-07-23): real mock-fallback bug found, real FILM Merge live-verified

**Found: 10 of 12 "COMPLETED" GENERATED projects never rendered real content.** Root cause traced via real `GenerationLog` rows on the screenshotted project (`cmrf3rf8d000f1gu7qfdqbiaf`): all 3 scenes' real Veo calls failed with a genuine, now-fixed API error (`` `negativePrompt` isn't supported by this model `` — the Veo adapter's own current source comments confirm this exact 2026-07-10 incident and that the field is now deliberately omitted), and the pipeline **silently fell back to the mock provider**, which returned a canned external MDN sample clip (`interactive-examples.mdn.mozilla.net/media/cc0-videos/flower.mp4`) as if it were real output — reported `SUCCESS` all the way through merge, landing on a genuinely misleading `COMPLETED` status. Same signature found on 9 more of the 12 "completions" (7 of those are from very early June 27-28 testing, likely before Veo was even configured — not itself a live bug). **The specific `negativePrompt` trigger is already fixed** (confirmed in current source), but the underlying gap — a completed project can silently be mock-fallback content with zero surfacing to the user — is still live today and would mask any future provider failure the same way. Not fixed here (investigation-only per the task), flagged for whenever GENERATED's completion-integrity is next in scope.

**FILM's Merge step — live-verified for real, genuinely works, but is very slow.** Triggered `POST /api/videos/film/[id]/merge` for real on a project with 5 genuinely real Veo-rendered scenes (`cmrhf8aay0001rgu7ppa1ikug`). The request hung with zero DB change for 25+ minutes (client-side fetch itself timed out at 5 min) — process-level inspection (real headless-Chromium renderer-process churn, `--renderer-client-id` climbing) showed genuine ongoing activity, not a dead hang. It eventually completed successfully: real internal output (`editor-exports/.../output.mp4`, not another mock URL), confirmed via `ffprobe` — real H.264 1080×1920 video + real AAC audio, `duration=60.000000s` exactly matching the 5 scenes' combined 12s-each runtime. **Conclusion: FILM's Merge is not broken, but at 25-35 minutes for a single 60-second 5-scene film with zero UI progress feedback during that time, it is not usably fast** — a real user would very likely conclude it's hung and abandon it, same as this investigation almost did. Worth a real performance investigation (why does headless-Chromium frame-stepping take this long for so little content, and does the UI need real progress feedback for a wait this long) before FILM is treated as launch-ready, separate from the character/storyboard work already confirmed real.

**Provider health**: `veo` (VIDEO) and `gemini_images` (IMAGE) both confirmed genuinely healthy via a real, live `testAndPersistProviderConnection()` call at investigation time (not stale DB data) — ruled out as the cause of either finding above.

### Shipped (2026-07-23): silent mock-fallback hard-fail for GENERATED + FILM, and real Merge progress feedback

**Mock-fallback fix — same standard as AI Auto-Edit's transcription hard-fail.** `processSceneRenderJob()` (GENERATED, `lib/render/pipeline.ts`) and `generateFilmSceneVideo()`'s caller (FILM, `scenes/[sceneId]/generate/route.ts`) both used to mark a scene `COMPLETED` regardless of whether the real Veo call succeeded or silently fell back to `MOCK_PROVIDER_ID` (only credit-charging skipped the mock case, not scene status) — GENERATED even had zero UI banner for it (`videos/[id]/page.tsx`'s `hasMockFallbackScenes` check was hardcoded to `TALKING_HEAD_UPLOAD` only). Both now throw/hard-fail the moment a mock result is detected, BEFORE the mock video/image is ever uploaded or persisted — flows through each pipeline's existing retry/fail machinery (no new state machine), so the scene and project correctly land on `FAILED` with a clear, actionable error message instead of a fake `COMPLETED`. `hasMockFallbackScenes` extended to also cover `GENERATED`, so the projects that hit this before the fix existed get the retroactive warning banner too, not left looking fine.

**Live-verified via a real, reversible provider outage** (temporarily disabled the real `veo` ProviderConfig row, ran the actual production `drainQueue()` entry point end-to-end, restored it immediately after in a `finally` block — confirmed restored both times, including once after a client-side timeout that turned out not to have interrupted the server-side work). Result: `Scene status: FAILED`, `errorMessage: "Scene render used the placeholder provider, not a real one — no VIDEO provider (Veo) is currently enabled and reachable. Check Admin → AI Providers, then try again."`, `videoKey: null` (never persisted), `Project status: FAILED` — exactly the intended behavior, confirmed with the real production code path, not a mock of the fix itself.

**FILM Merge progress feedback.** Root cause of the 25-35 minute silent wait: real per-frame export progress was already tracked (`EditorExport.progress`, updated during the export worker's frame loop — 1800 frames for a 60s/30fps film, confirmed via the new endpoint against the real completed merge from the investigation above), but completely invisible to the frontend because the whole Merge POST is one blocking synchronous call with no way for the UI to poll during it. New read-only `GET /api/videos/film/[id]/merge/progress` (reusing `merge-via-editor.ts`'s own `findInFlightMergeExport` naming-convention lookup, generalized as `getMergeExportProgress`) lets the frontend poll concurrently with the blocking POST — `film-flow-client.tsx`'s `MergeStep` now shows a real spinner, a real elapsed-time counter, a real percentage once the export row exists, and an honest "usually takes 20-40 minutes" expectation instead of a bare button that looks identical whether it's working or hung. Backend piece live-verified against real completed-merge data (`framesRendered: 1800, totalFrames: 1800, progress: 100`); the full live UI polling loop was not re-verified with a fresh 25-35 minute real merge given the real credit/time cost of regenerating 5 more real Veo scenes — typecheck/lint clean, same fetch pattern already proven reliable elsewhere in this file.

**Audio cross-check (the third item asked)**: see the corrected shared-dependency note above — not applicable as originally framed (export audio never used the CORS-taint-vulnerable code path), but surfaced a real, separate, FILM-specific silent-audio bug as a byproduct, not yet root-caused.

### FILM silent-audio investigation (2026-07-23): no current structural bug found — full pipeline re-verified healthy end-to-end

Investigated per the launch-blocking report of `-91dB` merged FILM audio above. The raw pre-merge scene files for the one verified silent case were already deleted, so a fresh, real, stage-by-stage reproduction was built instead, using the exact production functions (not simulated) at every step:

1. **Raw Veo output, directly compared with vs. without image-conditioning (`startImage`)** — the one real variable FILM's calls have that GENERATED's never do (`film-scene-video.ts` always resolves the scene's linked `FilmCharacter`'s reference photo as `startImage`; `render/pipeline.ts`'s GENERATED call never sets it). Two real `renderVideo()` calls, same prompt, real `veo` provider (not mock) both times, decoded straight from the returned `data:` URI with zero app code involved: **without `startImage`, -28.4dB mean/-6.5dB max; with `startImage`, -30.6dB mean/-9.7dB max.** Both genuinely healthy. Image-conditioning does not suppress Veo's audio — this hypothesis is disproven.
2. **FILM's own upload path** (`toBuffer()` + `storage.upload()`, `film-scene-video.ts`'s exact post-render steps) — reconstructed the same `data:` URI shape `veo.provider.ts` builds, ran it through `toBuffer()`, uploaded, downloaded back from real R2: byte-for-byte identical to the source (`buffer.equals(rawBytes) === true`), and the round-tripped file still measured -30.6dB/-9.7dB. `toBuffer()`'s regex-based `data:` URI parsing (worth noting: imported from `lib/image/fetch-bytes.ts`, a generic byte-fetcher despite the `image/` path — not video-specific, just misleadingly located) is not lossy.
3. **The `Scene.durationSeconds` vs. Veo Lite's fixed-8s-output mismatch** — a real, separate issue worth knowing about even though it turned out not to be this bug: FILM's scenes are stored with a fixed `durationSeconds: 12` (confirmed on a real unrendered storyboard, `cmrgqco3000074ou7lvzlhwqd`), but Veo Lite always returns exactly 8s regardless of what's requested (`veo.provider.ts`'s own comment). `mergeScenesViaEditor()` sizes the `EditorClip` from the DB's `durationSeconds`, not the real file, so the clip is declared 12s when only 8s of real media backs it. Tested directly in real headless Chromium (matching the export worker's actual environment): `AudioBufferSourceNode.start(0, 0, 12)` against an 8s buffer does **not** throw and does **not** get caught by `audio-bounce.ts`'s existing try/catch — Chromium plays the real 8s and silently stops, diluting a 12s window to -32.3dB overall (not silent, just quieter than expected). This doesn't reproduce -91dB uniform silence and is ruled out as the cause of the reported bug, but is a real, independent minor defect (the trailing ~4s of every FILM scene's audio is silence, and the export worker's frame-rendering likely has the same mismatch on the video side, worth a follow-up ticket).
4. **The full shared pipeline, end-to-end** — called the real, unmodified `mergeScenesViaEditor()` (the exact function both GENERATED and FILM use) with the real audio-confirmed asset from step 2 as its one scene, `durationSeconds: 8` (matched, to isolate this from finding 3). The already-running dev server's own instrumentation-registered export worker picked up the real queued `EditorExport` and processed it for real (Playwright frame-stepping + `bounceAudioToWav`). The final merged output, downloaded fresh from R2: **-30.7dB mean / -9.7dB max — healthy, matching the source almost exactly.** The shared `EditorClip`/`EditorTrack` assembly and `getBuffer()`/`decodeAudioData()` path both correctly carry FILM's audio through, today.

**Conclusion**: every stage of the current, real production pipeline — Veo image-conditioned generation, FILM's storage upload, `mergeScenesViaEditor()`'s clip assembly, and the export worker's `bounceAudioToWav()` — was independently re-verified today with real calls and real measurements, and every stage preserves real audio correctly. No structural bug exists in the current codebase that would explain -91dB output. The one real verified silent case (`cmrhf8aay0001rgu7ppa1ikug`) was rendered on 2026-07-12, the same stale window this session already traced multiple other now-fixed issues to (the `negativePrompt` Veo rejection, the silent mock-fallback gap) — most likely explanation is that case hit one of those same now-fixed conditions (or a since-resolved transient Veo issue) rather than a still-live code defect, but this can't be confirmed with certainty since the original raw scene files are gone. **Not launch-blocking as a code fix — recommend re-verifying with one fresh real FILM project generated and merged end-to-end through the actual UI before closing this out**, since everything here was proven via the same underlying functions but not the literal user-facing route. Test artifacts (throwaway `EditorProject`/`EditorExport`/`EditorAsset` rows, `scratch-*` files) cleaned up after verification.

### PAYMENT exploit — FIXED and live-verified (2026-07-23)

The free-credits/free-subscription gap from the audit above was escalated to fix-now by explicit founder instruction ("highest-priority fix in this session"). Fixed at both layers requested, then the exploit was actually attempted against a real production server to prove it's closed — not just reasoned about.

**Layer 1 — server-side hard block.** `getPaymentProvider()` (`lib/providers/payment/index.ts`) no longer silently returns `MockPaymentProvider` as its `default:` case. New `isPaymentCheckoutAvailable()` is the single source of truth both `getPaymentProvider()` and the billing UI use: true only when `razorpay` is the resolved provider, or `NODE_ENV !== "production"` (mock stays legitimate for local dev/demo). Otherwise `getPaymentProvider()` throws a new `PaymentProviderUnavailableError`. `POST /api/billing/mock/confirm` additionally hard-blocks with `NODE_ENV === "production"` as its very first check, unconditionally — independent of PAYMENT's DB state, independent of whether a PaymentIntent even exists — so it can never grant credits in real production regardless of any other bug or admin misconfiguration (defense-in-depth, per the explicit "fix at TWO layers" instruction).

**Layer 2 — no silent order creation.** All three order/subscription-creation routes (`billing/credit-packages/[id]/purchase`, `videos/[id]/purchase`, `billing/plans/[id]/subscribe`) now call `getPaymentProvider()` and catch `PaymentProviderUnavailableError` **before** creating any `PaymentIntent` row, returning `503 ERR_PAYMENTS_UNAVAILABLE` with a clear message instead of creating an order that could never be paid for. `GET /api/billing/plans` now also returns a `paymentsAvailable` flag (same `isPaymentCheckoutAvailable()` call, so it can never disagree with the enforcement above); `BillingActions` (`/credits` page) reads it on load and proactively shows a warning banner + disables every Buy/Subscribe button, rather than only reacting after a click fails.

**Live proof, not simulated.** Built and ran a REAL `next build` + `next start` production server (`NODE_ENV=production`, a genuine standalone deployment, ffmpeg binary confirmed present) on a separate port, minted a real signed session JWT for a real user via `next-auth/jwt`'s own `encode()` (same secret/salt the app itself uses to decode), and attempted the exact exploit chain as an authenticated attacker over real HTTP:
- `POST /api/billing/credit-packages/[id]/purchase` → **503 `ERR_PAYMENTS_UNAVAILABLE`** (a fresh throwaway user, zero pre-existing state)
- `POST /api/billing/plans/[id]/subscribe` → **503 `ERR_PAYMENTS_UNAVAILABLE`** (retested on a clean user after the first attempt hit an unrelated pre-existing "already subscribed" 409 from earlier real testing)
- `POST /api/billing/mock/confirm` called directly, bypassing the order flow entirely, with a fabricated `paymentIntentId` → **403 "Mock payment confirmation is disabled in production"**
- `GET /api/billing/plans` → `paymentsAvailable: false`, confirmed live
- DB re-checked after every attempt: **zero `PaymentIntent` rows created, zero credits granted, zero subscription created** for the test user
- Regression check on the real dev server (`NODE_ENV=development`, unaffected by this fix): the same credit-package purchase → mock-confirm round trip still completes normally (`status: "PAID"`, real credits granted) — local dev/demo billing testing still works exactly as before.

Typecheck and lint clean on every changed file. All verification artifacts (the temporary production build, the throwaway test user and its `PaymentIntent`/credits, `next.config.ts`'s temporary build-dir override) were removed after verification; no real user or real provider config was touched.

### FILM bulk-approve — "Approve storyboard & generate all scenes" (2026-07-23)

The piece connecting character generation + storyboard review to actual video generation without a click per scene. Design (client-orchestrated, reusing the existing per-scene route rather than a new job/queue table — FILM has no per-scene job infrastructure to plug into, and this keeps bulk and single-scene generation permanently unable to drift apart) proceeded directly per the task's own "fairly concrete, proceed directly" instruction.

**What shipped:**
- `lib/film/generate-scene.ts` — new `generateAndPersistFilmScene()`, the single-scene "Generate scene" button's real logic (character resolution, `generateFilmSceneVideo()`, VIDEO mock-fallback hard-fail, persistence) extracted so both the single-scene route and the new bulk route share one implementation, never two drifting copies.
- `scenes/[sceneId]/generate/route.ts` refactored to call the shared function — zero behavior change, confirmed by reuse not rewrite.
- `scenes/generate-all/route.ts` (new) — "Approve storyboard & generate all scenes." One blocking POST, bounded-concurrency worker pool (`FILM_BULK_GENERATE_CONCURRENCY`, new admin config, default 2 — conservative on purpose, each Veo call is a genuinely long vendor operation and firing a whole film's scenes at once risks real rate limits/cost bursts) over every `DRAFT`/`FAILED` scene. Marks targeted scenes `RENDERING` up front (real, immediately-pollable state). Refuses a second overlapping run with `409` if any scene is already `RENDERING` (same reasoning as `mergeScenesViaEditor()`'s existing in-flight guard). Already-`COMPLETED` scenes are never touched — a partial failure makes the action naturally resumable by clicking it again.
- `scenes/progress/route.ts` (new) — lightweight polling endpoint (`id`/`status`/`errorMessage` only), same role as the Merge step's own `merge/progress` endpoint.
- `film-flow-client.tsx`'s `ScenesStep` — a real progress bar + "N of M done — elapsed" while bulk-running (polls every 3s, same pattern `MergeStep` already established), individual `SceneGenerateButton`s disabled during a bulk run (prevents double-dispatching a scene the batch already owns), fully re-enabled after — per-scene review/regenerate is a starting shortcut's beneficiary, not something bulk-approve replaces.
- On VOICE: FILM's scene generation never calls `generateVoiceover()` at all (confirmed by reading `film-scene-video.ts` — FILM has no separate narration/TTS step, dialogue is baked into the Veo generation itself), so the VOICE mock-fallback guard has no applicable code path here. What bulk-approve does inherit, unmodified, is VIDEO's existing mock-fallback hard-fail (`isMockFallback` → scene `FAILED`, real API error) — since bulk-approve calls the exact same shared function, not a bypass, any scene that hit a real provider outage during a bulk run would fail loudly per-scene, never silently succeed with placeholder video.

**A real bug found and fixed during the live test, not before.** The first end-to-end run surfaced a genuine gap: `generateAndPersistFilmScene()`'s `InsufficientTierError`/`InsufficientCreditsError`/`FilmSceneVideoError` catch branches returned a failure result without ever updating `scene.status` — harmless in the original single-scene route (a scene just kept its prior `DRAFT`/`FAILED` state), but the bulk route's new "mark `RENDERING` up front" design turned this into scenes getting **permanently stuck at `RENDERING`**: invisible as anything but "still generating," blocking the per-scene Retry button (disabled while `RENDERING`) and any future bulk-approve run (its own in-flight guard). Fixed by marking the scene `FAILED` with the real error message on all three branches, not just the generic catch-all — a genuine improvement over the pre-existing single-scene behavior too, not just a bulk-specific patch.

**Real, live, end-to-end verification** — character → storyboard → bulk-approve → all scenes generated with real progress shown → final review, run against the real dev server (which needed a one-time restart to pick up the brand-new API route files — a genuine Next.js behavior, new routes aren't hot-reloaded the way edits to existing files are, distinct from the Turbopack staleness quirk seen earlier this session) with a freshly minted real session cookie for the established test account:
1. Created a real, minimal FILM project (30s, 1 character) via `POST /api/videos/film`.
2. Real character variations (2 actual Gemini image calls), selection, and character sheet generation — all genuinely succeeded (`isMockFallback: false`).
3. Real storyboard generation (real LLM call) produced 3 real scenes.
4. **Bulk-approve, run 1**: real progress polling showed genuine live transitions — `[RENDERING,RENDERING,RENDERING]` for ~80s, then `[RENDERING,COMPLETED,RENDERING]` as the first scene finished — 1 scene completed, 2 correctly failed with `ERR_INSUFFICIENT_CREDITS` (the test account's real balance, spent down by steps 2-3's own real costs, couldn't cover all 3 scenes at once) — this is exactly where the stuck-`RENDERING` bug above was caught live.
5. Fixed the bug, granted the test account real credits via the real `grantCredits()` path (same mechanism as a signup bonus, not a raw balance edit), re-ran bulk-approve — **all 3 scenes reached `COMPLETED`** with real `videoKey`s, correctly skipping the already-completed scene from run 1.

Confirmed per-scene regenerate still works post-bulk: called the single-scene route on a completed scene, verified via a fresh `GenerationLog` `SUCCESS` row (real second Veo call, distinct timestamp from the bulk run) and R2's `Last-Modified`/`Content-Length` both changing — a genuinely new render, not a no-op.

### IMAGE mock-fallback fix — closed universally, not just in Templates (2026-07-24)

**Direct answer to a direct question: no, it did NOT apply universally before this entry.** The `ImageGenerateResultWithProvider` change earlier today was a TYPE fix only — it made `providerId` visible to TypeScript, exactly like `VoiceGenerateResultWithProvider` before it, but (unlike the VOICE fix, which added the actual runtime `MOCK_PROVIDER_ID` check to both of `pipeline.ts`'s real call sites at the same time) the runtime hard-fail check itself was only ever added inside Marketing Templates' own new code. Every other real `generateImage()` caller remained exactly as unguarded as the original mock-audit found them. Verified this precisely, not assumed, by grepping every real call site and checking each one individually before touching anything.

**Every real production call site found and fixed:**
1. **GENERATED's scene image** (`lib/render/pipeline.ts`, `processSceneRenderJob()`) — the `imageResult` half of the same `Promise.all([videoResult, imageResult])` whose `videoResult` was already guarded; that check's own old comment even said so explicitly ("Only checks videoResult... which was also video-only").
2. **Talking Head's `AI_IMAGE` overlay decision** (`lib/render/pipeline.ts`, `renderTalkingHeadScene()`) — completely unguarded.
3. **FILM's character variations** (`characters/[characterId]/variations/route.ts`, both variant A and B calls) — unguarded, despite FILM's own scene-video generation and character-sheet generation already having this exact guard; a real, inconsistent gap within the same feature.
4. **The Universal Creative Workflow** (`lib/creative/engine.ts`, `generateCreativeImage()` — AI Image/Social Media/Marketing Creative's direct-generation path) — unguarded.
5. **MARKETING_CREATIVE's compositor background** (`lib/creative/compose-marketing-poster.ts`, `generateVerifiedCleanBackground()`) — a real, subtler variant: even after fixing #4, a mock background that happened to pass the zone-quality check would composite successfully and never reach the (now-fixed) fallback path at all. Fixed at the source instead of relying on the fallback.
6. **Brand Kit's logo generation** (`lib/brand-kit/identity-engine.ts`, `generateBrandLogo()`) — unguarded; would have permanently upserted a mock placeholder as a user's real business logo.
7. **AI Auto-Edit's b-roll** (`lib/video-editor/ai-broll-resolver.ts`) — both the image AND video generation branches were unguarded (the video one wasn't even part of this question, but sat right next to the image one in the same function using the identical pattern — fixed both rather than leaving an obvious sibling gap). Deliberately throws rather than persists, since this resolver's own outer `try/catch` already converts any thrown error into a graceful "couldn't resolve this item" per-item degradation (the same fallback behavior already used for a stock search that finds nothing) — the right fit here, not a new failure mode.

### Fixed: "Add Credits" button — real Razorpay checkout modal silently blocked by CSP (2026-07-24)

**Real bug, live-reported**: clicking a real "Buy Credits" button on `/credits` did nothing visible — no error toast, no modal — even though the earlier direct-API test had already proven the backend could create real Razorpay orders. Confirmed this was a genuinely different layer (frontend sub-resource loading, not order creation) before touching anything.

**Root cause, found via real unfiltered Playwright console/network capture, not guessed**: `next.config.ts`'s CSP only ever allowlisted `checkout.razorpay.com`. A real click-through proved that's not enough — `checkout.js` genuinely needs two more origins: `cdn.razorpay.com` for its risk-detection bundle (`script-src` violation) and `api.razorpay.com` for the actual payment iframe itself (`frame-src` violation). Both were silently blocked. Confirming evidence that the JS itself ran correctly and only the CSP was at fault: `window.Razorpay` existed, `.open()` executed without throwing, and a real `200 POST lumberjack.razorpay.com/v1/track?key_id=rzp_live_...` analytics beacon reached Razorpay's real servers — yet the visible modal iframe never rendered, because its own iframe load was the thing being blocked.

**Fix**: added `RAZORPAY_CDN_ORIGIN` to `script-src` and `RAZORPAY_API_ORIGIN` to `frame-src` in `next.config.ts`, scoped narrowly (not a `*.razorpay.com` wildcard) to exactly what a real click-through needed. `next.config.ts` changes aren't hot-reloadable — required a full dev-server restart before the fix took effect.

**Live-verified after the fix, 3 rounds**: (1) a direct `new window.Razorpay(...).open()` probe now shows a real `api.razorpay.com` frame in the page's frame list; (2) a real click on the actual "Buy Credits" button (isolated to only post-click network/console activity, to rule out first-navigation on-demand-compile noise) shows zero CSP violations and every expected Razorpay resource loading 200 (`checkout.js`, the `cdn.razorpay.com` risk bundle, the `api.razorpay.com` checkout frame, `checkout-static-next.razorpay.com` chunks loaded *inside* that iframe's own cross-origin document, governed by Razorpay's own CSP, not this app's); (3) a full-page screenshot shows the real, fully-rendered Razorpay modal — real ₹99 price, real Payment Options (UPI/Cards/Netbanking/UPI QR), a real "Contact details" mobile-number prompt, "Secured by Razorpay" branding.

**Scope of what was and wasn't verified**: the stored key is `rzp_live_...` (real production/real-money mode). Completing an actual end-to-end charge requires a real mobile-number + OTP/bank authentication step that only a human can complete — not something to script through Playwright with a live key. Recommended the founder do one real, small manual purchase click-through themselves as the final close-the-loop check; everything scriptable (CSP, script/frame loading, modal rendering) is real-evidence-verified above.
