### Real vendor duration caps investigated (2026-07-24) — confirmed via each vendor's own current docs, not assumption

| Provider | Real single-call max | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Veo 3.1 (incl. Lite) | 8 seconds, fixed — Lite doesn't support the extension workaround at all | ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/veo |
| Seedance2.ai | 15 seconds (4-15s range) | seedance2.ai/api-docs |

Neither can produce one continuous 20s clip in a single call — reaching 20s always means stitching ≥2 clips via the existing merge pipeline, regardless of provider. This directly informed the app-level cap and FILM duration-selector work below.

### App-level 20-second hard cap on every video generation (2026-07-24)

New `lib/video-generation-limits.ts` — `MAX_VIDEO_GENERATION_TOTAL_SECONDS = 20`, deliberately a plain exported constant, NOT wired into `CONFIG_REGISTRY` like almost everything else admin-editable in this codebase: a real "hard cap" per the founder's own wording, not a business/pricing knob an admin should be able to quietly raise. Confirmed with the founder this applies to a generation's TOTAL output duration, not just a single vendor call (their explicit correction to my initial "per-call only" proposal) — so it also caps GENERATED's and FILM's full stitched/multi-scene runtime, not just one clip.

**Enforced at 4 real chokepoints**:
1. `renderVideo()` itself (`lib/generation/video.ts`) — universal defense-in-depth catching every caller (Quick Video, GENERATED per-scene, FILM per-scene, Marketing Templates, AI Auto-Editor b-roll) with zero per-flow duplication. Live-verified: throws `VideoDurationCapExceededError` for a 25s request, passes a 20s request through to the real (unrelated) failure beyond the cap check.
2. GENERATED's `useSceneSplit` path (`lib/scenes/engine.ts`) — the LLM freely decides scene count (real, observed range 3-5) at a fixed 8s/scene, previously reaching 24-40s uncapped. Now hard-trimmed to however many whole scenes actually fit (2 scenes × 8s = 16s max) — real, deterministic enforcement, not just a prompt instruction.
3. GENERATED's proportional-allocation path (`app/api/videos/route.ts`) — every seeded `Template.durationSeconds` is 30 (confirmed live, exceeding the cap); now clamped to the 20s ceiling before scene-duration allocation.
4. FILM's storyboard planner (`lib/creative/film-storyboard.ts`) — see below.

### FILM: scene-count selector → duration selector (2026-07-24)

**Correction to the original premise**: investigated first, and FILM never actually had a "pick 1-5 scenes" selector — it already used a total-DURATION selector (60/90/120/180/300s, labeled in minutes). The real work was narrowing that existing selector's range, not building a new control type.

**Clarified with the founder before building**: does the 20s cap apply per-call or to FILM's total stitched output? My initial proposal (per-call only, FILM exempt up to 60s) was corrected — the founder confirmed the cap applies to FILM's total too. `DURATION_OPTIONS` narrowed to exactly `{10s, 20s}` (`create/film/page.tsx`), `createFilmProjectSchema.durationSeconds` narrowed to `z.union([z.literal(10), z.literal(20)])`.

**Real math, reported before building**: at 8-12s/scene (Veo/Seedance-compatible range), a 10s target is almost always exactly 1 scene; a 20s target is almost always exactly 2. The storyboard system prompt now says this explicitly (was previously asking for open-ended "8 to 12 seconds long... add up to approximately the total duration" against a 30-600s range). Real enforcement, not just prompt-following: new `trimScenesToTotalDuration()` hard-trims whatever the LLM actually returns to fit within the target, always keeping at least 1 scene (clamped down if needed) — **live-verified with 5 synthetic adversarial cases** (LLM ignoring instructions and returning 3-4 scenes for a 10-20s target) — all correctly trimmed to comply, never exceeding target, never empty.

**Real quality fix found along the way**: GENERATED's own `scene-split.ts` had the identical structural problem — its LLM was asked for "3 to 5" scenes (real, observed range), which `createScenesFromSplit`'s new hard cap (item 2, #2 above) truncates to first-N — but that truncation could silently drop the ad's closing/farewell beat, which the system prompt's own rule 4 explicitly says must never be dropped. Fixed at the source: the prompt now asks for exactly 2 scenes (hook + close) instead of 3-5, so the real cap and the real prompt now agree — no reliance on truncation order preserving the right content.

**FILM storyboard generation itself could not be live-tested against a real LLM call** — blocked by the same real, currently-live dual-LLM-provider outage documented below (item 0), not a code issue; verified via direct unit testing of the enforcement logic instead (5/5 adversarial cases correct).

### Prompt-engineering: "every second must earn its place" (2026-07-24)

Strengthened 3 real generation prompts with explicit no-filler/high-impact-ad language: FILM's storyboard system prompt (`film-storyboard.ts`), GENERATED's scene-split system prompt (`scene-split.ts` — also narrowed from 3-5 to exactly 2 scenes per the cap work above), and Quick Video's prompt builder (`quick-video-prompt.ts`). ### Charge-before-generation, real refund-on-failure (2026-07-24)

Investigated first: all 3 flows (Quick Video, GENERATED, FILM) used the same precheck-then-charge-AFTER-success pattern — credits were only ever deducted once a real render had already succeeded, meaning a user could in principle trigger many real generations without ever being charged if something failed after the vendor call but before the charge (or if the charge itself silently failed). Changed to reserve-at-submit, matching the founder's own cited precedent (Seedance2.ai's own vendor-credit system reserves on submit and refunds on failure).

**Real, already-anticipated pattern reused, not invented**: `grantCredits()`'s own `GrantInput.transactionType` field comment already said "a REFUND is booked as an ADMIN_ADJUSTMENT lot (there's no dedicated REFUND lot type) but should still read 'Refund'" — written into the schema/engine but never once actually called anywhere in the codebase until now. New `refundCredits()` (`lib/credits/engine.ts`) is a thin, named wrapper over exactly that pattern.

**Applied to all 3 flows** (`veo-lite-video.ts`, `film-scene-video.ts`, `pipeline.ts`'s `processSceneRenderJob`): credits reserved immediately after the tier/balance precheck, BEFORE the real vendor call; any failure after that point (render, upload, persist) triggers a full refund of the reservation; on success, a true-up settles the reservation against the REAL final cost (which can differ from what was reserved — a mock-fallback costs 0, or the provider-selector's failover can land on a differently-priced provider) — refunds the difference if over-reserved, charges the difference if under-reserved. GENERATED's version specifically handles the retry case: a failed-but-retrying scene refunds its reservation immediately rather than holding it across the retry, since the retry re-reserves fresh next attempt (holding it would have double-charged one scene across 2 attempts).

**Live-verified**: the `refundCredits()` primitive directly against the real DB (reserve 15 → real balance 116→101 → refund 15 → real balance back to 116, with a genuine `REFUND`-typed `CreditTransaction` row, not disguised as something else). **Could not verify the full integration with real non-zero numbers** — live DB shows the founder has deliberately zeroed every real video action cost (`veo_lite`, `film_scene`, `film`, `veo_standard`, `veo_multiscene_ad` all currently 0) for their own ongoing testing, confirmed explicitly earlier this session ("leave veo_lite at 0") — respected that and did not perturb it further, even temporarily. Forced-failure tests against the real 0-cost flows correctly showed zero balance movement either way (nothing to reserve, nothing to refund) — consistent, not a bug, but not a full proof of the non-zero path either; that's honestly flagged, not claimed as fully proven.

### Image generation "Couldn't enhance your prompt" — real root cause found, not a code bug (2026-07-24)

Reproduced live 3 times across this session (each ~90s-2hrs apart): **both of the app's 2 configured LLM providers are genuinely, persistently out of real prepaid credits/quota right now** — OpenAI: real `429 insufficient_quota` ("You exceeded your current quota, please check your plan and billing"); Gemini: real `429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` ("Your prepayment credits are depleted") on the most recent check, `503 UNAVAILABLE` ("high demand") on an earlier check — same underlying real credits-depleted condition manifesting as two different vendor error codes at different moments, not a one-off blip. Please try again." gave zero signal whether to retry or escalate; new `describeAllProvidersFailure()` (`lib/generation/types.ts`) distinguishes "temporarily overloaded, retry shortly" from "billing/quota exhausted, an admin needs to act" — used in `enhance-prompt/route.ts`'s catch block. Genuine, measurable difference every time: old output "camera then gracefully pulls back... warmly lit, traditional Indian sweet shop"; new output "A slow push-in... camera then smoothly tracks back... bathed in warm cinematic lighting with rich color grading" / "confident, subtle handheld drift... soft, warm rim lighting... premium golden hour lighting." ### Quick Video: real "no voice/no sound" bug found and fixed (2026-07-25)

Founder-reported real gap: an actual generated Quick Video came back completely silent despite the UI promising "speech and sound." Traced end-to-end: `route.ts` → `generateVeoLiteVideo()` → `renderVideo()` — no VOICE provider call, no music logic anywhere in the flow, 100% reliant on the video provider's own native audio.

**Real root cause, confirmed on the founder's own actual output file**: the most recent real `creative_video` generation was served by `seedance2` (Veo is currently disabled). Downloaded and ffprobed the real file — zero audio streams. `seedance.provider.ts` was sending `generate_audio: false` unconditionally, an unexplained oversight from this adapter's earlier rewrite this session — silently defeating every spoken-line prompt whenever Seedance serves the request, which is the common case right now. **Not Quick-Video-specific** — GENERATED and FILM's prompts also depend on native video-model speech, so this silently broke audio for all three flows. Fixed: `generate_audio: true`. Live-verified on a fresh real Seedance generation — real AAC stereo audio stream now present (was: video-only).

**Real, adjacent discovery while investigating "reuse GENERATED's pattern"**: `mergeScenesViaEditor()` (GENERATED's real merge/compositing function) never actually mixed in voice or music at all — `Scene.voiceKey` (real ElevenLabs narration) and `Scene.backgroundMusicUrl` were generated/assigned but silently dropped at merge time; only VIDEO + TEXT-overlay tracks were ever built. Confirmed with the founder before fixing (scope check) — fixed together: `mergeScenesViaEditor()` now builds a real AUDIO/VOICE track (per-scene clips) and a real AUDIO/MUSIC track (one clip spanning the full duration), using the same `AUDIO`/`VOICE`/`MUSIC` track kind/subtype the main Cloud Video Editor UI already supports — this was the one caller that never wired it up, not a missing Export Engine capability. `pipeline.ts` and FILM's merge route both updated to pass real `voiceKey`/`backgroundMusicUrl` through.

**Quick Video now gets real voice+music too**, reusing `mergeScenesViaEditor()` directly (a single-scene call, no new compositing logic) rather than duplicating it: `generateVeoLiteVideo()` generates a real ElevenLabs narration for the spoken line (hard-fails on mock-fallback, same standard as everywhere else), fetches the admin-configured `DEFAULT_BACKGROUND_MUSIC_URL`, and only runs the compositing step when there's actually something to composite (no real cost/latency added for the common no-speech/no-music case). **Real double-audio conflict caught and fixed**: since the video model can ALSO render native lip-synced speech from the prompt, adding a separate ElevenLabs track on top would create two competing voices — `quick-video-prompt.ts` no longer asks the video model to render the spoken line at all ("real narration is dubbed in separately, so the video itself should not attempt to render spoken audio"), matching GENERATED's own established convention of never asking the video model to voice dialogue. UI copy corrected to stop overpromising ("with speech and sound" → "with a real spoken voiceover when you add one below" — music was never something the user could control, so dropped from the promise).

**Live-verified, with one genuine, separate real blocker found**: the credit-refund primitive was already proven correct in an earlier turn (a real reserve→refund round-trip against the DB). A fresh real end-to-end attempt (real Seedance render + real ElevenLabs call) confirmed the wiring is correct — a real request reached ElevenLabs — but hit a real, external account limitation: `402 payment_required — "Free users cannot use library voices via the API. Please upgrade your subscription to use this voice."` This is a genuine ElevenLabs account/plan issue, not a code bug — flagged for the founder, not silently worked around. This same account limitation will also block a full live test of FILM's new voiceover pipeline (below) until resolved.

### Production Docker image missing Playwright/Chromium — real first-deploy crash, fixed (2026-07-25)

**Symptom**: first real Railway production boot crashed repeatedly with `Error: An error occurred while loading instrumentation hook: Failed to load external module playwright: Error: Cannot find module '/app/node_modules/playwright-core/browsers.json'`. The video editor's export renderer (`export-worker.ts`) statically imports `chromium` from `playwright`; that import chain is reached from `instrumentation.ts`'s startup sequence, so a broken Playwright install took the entire server down, not just exports.

**Root cause, confirmed by reading the Dockerfile, not assumed**: two independent gaps, both real. (1) The Dockerfile never ran `playwright install` anywhere — no stage ever downloaded a Chromium build at all. (2) Even a JS-only `playwright-core` package wasn't guaranteed to survive into the final image: `.next/standalone`'s file-tracing (`@vercel/nft`) only copies files it can statically resolve, and playwright-core resolves some of its own supporting files (`browsers.json` among them) dynamically — the exact same class of bug already hit and fixed for `ffmpeg-static`'s binary (see `next.config.ts`'s `outputFileTracingIncludes` comment). On top of both: the base image was `node:22-alpine`, and Playwright's Chromium build does not run on Alpine/musl at all — `--with-deps` shells out to `apt-get`, which doesn't exist there, and the browser binary itself is glibc-linked.

**Fix**: switched all three Dockerfile stages from `node:22-alpine` to `node:22-bookworm-slim` (Debian) — kept consistent across `deps`/`builder`/`runner` so `npm ci` resolves the matching glibc prebuilt of every native-binding package (`sharp` ships separate glibc/musl builds; mixing bases would've silently shipped the wrong one). Added an explicit whole-directory `COPY` of `node_modules/playwright` and `node_modules/playwright-core` from the builder stage into the runner (bypassing the tracer entirely, same fix pattern already used for `prisma` in this same file), then `RUN npx playwright install --with-deps chromium` directly in the final runtime stage — Chromium only, not the other Playwright browsers this app never uses, to keep image size sane. `PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH=0` keeps the downloaded browser inside `node_modules/playwright-core` (Playwright's own documented bundling pattern) instead of a separate top-level cache path. Explicit `chown` after install since the `RUN` executes as root, before the existing `USER nextjs` switch.

**Resilience fix, scoped narrowly**: wrapped just the export queue worker's dynamic import in `instrumentation.ts` in a try/catch — confirmed via grep that `export-worker.ts` is the *only* file in the codebase importing `playwright`, so no other startup worker is affected. Unlike the PAYMENT hard-boot-block two entries above (a deliberate hard stop — that category's silent failure was a live exploit), a broken export/render pipeline failing open just means exports don't process while the rest of the app (auth, dashboard, every other queue) keeps serving — matches this codebase's existing "PAYMENT alone gets the hard stop, everything else warns" posture instead of adding a second, inconsistent hard-stop category.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit` and `eslint src/instrumentation.ts` both clean. Not yet live-verified against a real Railway rebuild at time of writing (deploy was in flight) — confirm in the next deploy's build logs that `RUN npx playwright install --with-deps chromium` actually executes and downloads a browser (not skipped/cached-empty), and in the runtime logs that the `BOOT REFUSED`/playwright crash no longer appears.

**Follow-up (same day) — identical crash persisted after the above shipped.** Root-caused further: `export-worker.ts` had a static top-level `import { chromium } from "playwright"`, so merely *importing* the module (which `export-queue-worker.ts` does, which `instrumentation.ts` does on every boot) evaluated playwright-core's own module-init code — including its `browsers.json` read — regardless of the try/catch already wrapping the dynamic `import("@/lib/video-editor/export-queue-worker")` one level up in `instrumentation.ts`. The try/catch there was real but insufficiently deep: it only guards against the *outer* dynamic import failing, not a transitive static import several files down throwing during that same module evaluation — which in Node/webpack semantics it still should have caught via the rejected promise, so this may also indicate the previous Dockerfile fix hadn't actually been deployed yet (worth confirming Railway's build settings have "Builder" set to Dockerfile, not Nixpacks, since no `railway.json`/`railway.toml` in this repo forces that explicitly). Fixed at the root regardless: `chromium` is now imported lazily (`const { chromium } = await import("playwright")`) inside `renderExportJob` itself — the one function that actually launches a browser — while `Browser`/`Page` stay as `import type` (erased at compile time, zero runtime cost). Now nothing touches playwright's runtime code until an export job actually runs, and if Chromium is missing, the failure happens inside `renderExportJob`'s existing try/catch, which already calls `failExport()` with a real message — one export fails, nothing else does. Also added a build-time tripwire in the Dockerfile (`test -f .../browsers.json`, twice — right after the COPY and again after install) so a future regression here fails the BUILD loudly instead of shipping a silently broken image.

### Production migrate-deploy crash: `node_modules/.bin/prisma_schema_build_bg.wasm` ENOENT — real root cause, fixed (2026-07-26)

**Symptom**: `prisma migrate deploy` crashed at container startup with `ENOENT: /app/node_modules/.bin/prisma_schema_build_bg.wasm` — a path that's never existed anywhere in this project; the real wasm file lives at `node_modules/prisma/build/prisma_schema_build_bg.wasm`.

**Root cause, confirmed by reading the actual bundled source, not assumed**: `node_modules/prisma/build/index.js` loads its schema engine via `` `${__dirname}/prisma_schema_build_bg.wasm` `` — computed at runtime from wherever that executing file physically sits. `node_modules/.bin/prisma` is npm's shim/symlink to `../prisma/build/index.js`; on Linux npm creates this as a real symlink. Docker's `COPY`, when the *source* is a single file rather than a directory, **dereferences** a symlink — it copies the resolved target's actual bytes and writes them as a plain file at the destination, not a symlink. The old Dockerfile did exactly this: `COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules/.bin/prisma ./node_modules/.bin/prisma`. The result was a full, physically-relocated copy of `prisma/build/index.js`'s bundled code sitting at `node_modules/.bin/prisma` — a real file now, not a symlink — so `__dirname` for it genuinely was `node_modules/.bin`, and it looked for the wasm file right beside itself, where it never existed. The whole-directory copies of `node_modules/prisma` and `node_modules/@prisma` were never the problem; only the single-file `.bin` shim copy was.

**Fix**: removed the `.bin/prisma` COPY entirely and stopped invoking Prisma through any shim in this image. Both the Dockerfile's `CMD` and `docker-compose.yml`'s `command:` now call the real entry file directly — `node node_modules/prisma/build/index.js migrate deploy` — the same file the shim itself would have `exec`'d, just without the broken indirection. Verified locally that this entry-file invocation produces identical output to `npx prisma --version`. Also added a matching build-time tripwire (`test -f .../prisma_schema_build_bg.wasm`) alongside the existing Playwright one. Moving `migrate deploy` into the Dockerfile's own `CMD` (previously only `node server.js`, with migrations left to a docker-compose-only override) is also a real behavior change worth knowing: a Railway deployment with no custom Start Command override will now run migrations automatically on every boot; a deployment that already has a custom Start Command configured to mirror the old broken invocation still needs that override updated the same way, since an explicit Start Command always wins over the image's `CMD`.

**Follow-up (same investigation) — a second, different missing-module crash after the wasm fix**: `migrate deploy` next failed with `Cannot find module 'fast-check'`, required via `@prisma/config/node_modules/effect/dist/cjs/FastCheck.js`. Confirmed by reading the actual `package.json` files, not assumed: `@prisma/config` (new in Prisma 7 — it's what powers `prisma.config.ts`) has real, required dependencies on `c12`, `deepmerge-ts`, `effect`, and `empathic`; `effect` itself has a real, required dependency on `fast-check`. All five of those packages are hoisted by npm to the true root `node_modules/`, entirely outside both the `node_modules/prisma` and `node_modules/@prisma` trees the Dockerfile was copying. `npm ci` had installed everything correctly the whole time — the Dockerfile's selective per-package COPY strategy was the gap, and it was a **second, independent instance of the same class of gap** the wasm fix above had already hit once. Enumerating Prisma's CLI transitive dependencies by hand is fragile in a way that will keep resurfacing across Prisma minor versions.

**Fix**: replaced every selective `node_modules/prisma` + `node_modules/@prisma` + `node_modules/playwright` + `node_modules/playwright-core` copy with one full `COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/node_modules ./node_modules` — copying output an already-real `npm ci` produced, not installing anything inside the image. This permanently closes the "missing transitive CLI dependency" bug class rather than patching it one package at a time. Added a third, stronger build-time tripwire on top of the existing file-existence checks: `RUN node node_modules/prisma/build/index.js --version`, which exercises the CLI's entire real module-resolution chain (the exact path `migrate deploy` takes) at build time, without needing a live database — verified locally, exits 0. Traded a larger final image for eliminating this bug class outright; no other option was considered since the per-package approach had already failed twice.

**Follow-up (same investigation) — a third, different crash after the full-node_modules fix**: `migrate deploy` now failed with `Error: The datasource.url property is required in your Prisma config file when using prisma migrate deploy`, despite `prisma.config.ts` correctly declaring `datasource: { url: env("DATABASE_URL") } }` and `docker-compose.yml` correctly setting a real `DATABASE_URL`. Confirmed by reading `@prisma/config`'s actual bundled `env()` implementation (`process.env[name]`, throws `PrismaConfigEnvError` if falsy — a plain synchronous read, nothing exotic) and by reading `schema.prisma`'s `datasource db {}` block, which has **no `url` field at all** — Prisma 7 moved the connection string out of the schema entirely, making `prisma.config.ts` the *only* place it can come from. Root cause: `prisma.config.ts` is a root-level file, a sibling of `package.json` — not part of the `/app/prisma` directory the Dockerfile already copied, and never referenced by any `COPY` line at all. `.next/standalone`'s tracer had no reason to include it either, since only the separate Prisma CLI process imports it, never the Next.js app itself. **Reproduced locally, not just inferred**: temporarily moving `prisma.config.ts` aside (with `env()` and `DATABASE_URL` both left completely untouched) and running `migrate status` produced the exact reported error verbatim. Also confirmed neither `prisma --version` nor `prisma validate` would have caught this — both succeed with the config file entirely absent, since neither needs a connection string; only `migrate deploy`/`migrate status` actually validate `datasource.url`.

**Fix**: added `COPY --from=builder /app/prisma.config.ts ./prisma.config.ts` and a matching `test -f` build-time tripwire (the `--version` tripwire's own comment was corrected at the same time — it was overstating what that check actually proves).

**Follow-up (same investigation) — copying prisma.config.ts correctly then broke the build itself**: the existing `RUN node node_modules/prisma/build/index.js --version` tripwire started failing with `Cannot resolve environment variable: DATABASE_URL`. Root cause, confirmed by reading `@prisma/config`'s actual `env()` source (`process.env[name]`, throws `PrismaConfigEnvError` if falsy) and reproduced locally twice: (1) with `prisma.config.ts` present but no `.env` files and no `DATABASE_URL` anywhere (moved `.env.local` aside temporarily to match the runner stage exactly) — `prisma --version` fails with the identical error, because the config file's top-level `datasource: { url: env("DATABASE_URL") } }` evaluates unconditionally the moment the CLI loads the config, for every subcommand, not just ones needing a live connection; (2) setting a placeholder `DATABASE_URL` in that same no-`.env`-files environment makes it succeed. Before the `prisma.config.ts` copy fix, `--version` had succeeded in the runner stage for an unrelated reason — the config file wasn't there *at all*, so there was no module to evaluate; copying it correctly (necessary and correct) surfaced this as a new, second-order consequence.

**Fix**: added `ENV DATABASE_URL="postgresql://placeholder:placeholder@placeholder:5432/placeholder"` in the runner stage, right before the tripwire block — the same placeholder value and reasoning already used in the builder stage since the very first Dockerfile draft, never a problem there for the identical reason: real deployments (docker-compose's `environment:`, Railway's variable reference) always set a real `DATABASE_URL` at container *runtime*, which overrides any image-baked `ENV` the same way `docker run -e` always wins. Nothing at build time ever attempts a real connection with this value.

### Installation Wizard: replaced phone-OTP with email+password for the Super Admin step (MVP, 2026-07-27)

**Why**: the Super Admin step (`install-wizard.tsx`'s `AdminStep`) required phone-OTP verification (`signIn("otp", ...)` + `POST /api/install/promote-admin`) to create the very first account on a fresh install — a real chicken-and-egg problem on a VPS with no SMS vendor configured yet. Explicit founder decision to replace it with direct email+password creation for the MVP, without touching phone-OTP for any other flow.

**Schema**: `User.passwordHash String?` added (migration `20260726184724_add_user_password_hash`) — nullable, so every existing phone-OTP/Google account is unaffected. Stored as `"saltHex:hashHex"` via Node's built-in `crypto.scrypt` (new `src/lib/security/password.ts`, `hashPassword`/`verifyPassword`) — no new dependency, matching this codebase's existing `security/` helpers (`encryption.ts`, `master-key.ts`) already using `crypto` directly rather than a third-party library like bcrypt (also sidesteps re-opening the native-binding/musl-vs-glibc class of Docker issues this project just spent a full session fixing for `sharp`/Playwright).

**New auth path, additive only**: a `"password"` Credentials provider (`lib/auth/index.ts`) — looks up by email, verifies against `passwordHash`, returns `null` for any account without one (so phone-OTP/Google accounts can never authenticate through it). New `POST /api/install/create-admin` route creates the account directly with `role: "ADMIN"` in one step (guarded by the same `isInstalled()` flag `promote-admin` already used, so it can never be called again post-install — never a privilege-escalation backdoor), then the client calls `signIn("password", ...)` to establish the session. Since the account is created with `role: "ADMIN"` from the start, the JWT's role is correct from the first sign-in — no separate `update({role: "ADMIN"})` trick needed the way the old OTP-based promotion required.

**Scope decision, confirmed with the founder rather than assumed**: password login is also exposed as a second, minimal option on the main `/login` page (a toggle below the existing phone/Google flow) — without it, a password-based admin would have no durable way back in once their session expired, since `/login` previously had no password option at all. Phone-OTP and Google sign-in on `/login` are completely unchanged; this is additive.

**Not built**: a "Business details" step — the requirements listed it as "(if applicable)"; the Super Admin is a platform-owner account, not a business/customer account (that's what the separate, already-existing `(auth)/onboarding` page collects post-login, unrelated to this flow), so it doesn't apply here.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit`, `eslint` on every changed file, and `vitest run` (135 files / 3330 tests) all clean. Full `npm run build` succeeded (`/install` and `/login` both compiled). Additionally live-verified beyond static checks: a real round-trip of `hashPassword`/`verifyPassword` (correct password verifies, wrong password rejected, two hashes of the same password differ via salting, a malformed stored value is handled safely) and the full create-then-authorize path against the real local dev database (schema validation accepts/rejects correctly, a real user row is created with `role: "ADMIN"` and a non-plaintext `passwordHash`, the password-provider's exact `authorize()` logic correctly accepts the right password/role and rejects a wrong password or nonexistent account) — test data cleaned up afterward, real `isInstalled()` production flag never touched.

### Production `/install` → Storage → Test & Save crash: `EACCES: /app/.encryption-key` — fixed (2026-07-27)

**Symptom**: saving any provider credential (surfaced via R2 storage config, but affects every category) crashed with `Error: EACCES: permission denied, open '/app/.encryption-key'`. Not an R2/credentials problem — the app never got as far as talking to R2.

**Root cause, confirmed by reading `master-key.ts` and the Dockerfile together**: `getMasterKey()`'s file-based fallback (used whenever `CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY` isn't set) wrote to `join(process.cwd(), ".encryption-key")` — directly under `/app`, the Dockerfile's `WORKDIR`. The runner stage runs as a non-root user (`USER nextjs`), and `/app` itself is root-owned from the earlier `COPY` steps (none of them `--chown` the bare directory, only specific subpaths inside it) — a non-root user can't create a *new* top-level file in a root-owned directory, only read/write files that already exist there. A brand-new container (no key file baked into the image, by design — it's gitignored) hit this the first time any credential was saved.

**Fix**: new keys now write under a dedicated `/app/.data/` subdirectory instead, which the Dockerfile explicitly creates and `chown`s to `nextjs:nodejs` with real permissions (`0700` on the directory, `0600` on the key file — no `chmod 777` anywhere). `readKeyFile()` still checks the *old* root-level path first, purely so any already-generated key (this dev machine's real one included) keeps decrypting the exact same `ProviderConfig` rows it always has — confirmed live, read-only, without touching the real file. The "generate if missing, write to the new path" behavior was verified separately in a fully isolated scratch directory (no legacy file present, simulating a fresh container) — correctly falls back to `.data/`, produces a valid 32-byte key, and the file's on-disk content matches what was returned. Encryption itself was never disabled; only the fallback file's location and the directory's ownership changed.

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit`, `eslint`, `vitest run` (135/135, 3330/3330), and `npm run build` all clean. Docker-level permission behavior (the actual non-root write) can only be proven inside a real container rebuild, not this dev machine — flagged, not asserted, as the one thing to confirm after the next `docker compose build --no-cache && up -d` on the VPS: `/install` → Storage → Test & Save should succeed with no `EACCES`.

### Full founder-journey E2E dry run (fresh install → dashboard → project creation → session persistence) — 2 real bugs found and fixed (2026-07-27)

**Method, not just code reading**: created a genuinely fresh, isolated Postgres database (`elevatex_ai_e2e_fresh`, on the same local Postgres container this project already uses, dropped afterward — the real dev database was never touched), migrated + seeded it from zero, and drove the *entire* founder journey via real HTTP requests (cookie-jar session continuity, real CSRF handshakes) against the actual production entrypoint — `node .next/standalone/server.js` with explicit env vars, not `next dev` and not `next start` (which itself warned it's incompatible with `output: standalone`) — since that's what the real Docker container runs.

**False alarm investigated and resolved, not asserted either way**: `/install` appeared to keep rendering the wizard (HTTP 200) even after `POST /api/install/finish` succeeded and the DB flag was confirmed `true`. Root-caused via `curl -i`'s raw response: Next.js had already started streaming the page (200) before `ensureNotInstalled()`'s `redirect()` fired, so it embedded the redirect as an RSC digest + `<meta http-equiv="refresh">` fallback instead of a top-level 3xx — invisible to `curl`, which doesn't execute JS. Proved this with a real headless Chromium session (Playwright, cookies injected): it correctly cascades `/install` → `/login` → (already authenticated) → `/onboarding`. Not a bug — a blind spot in HTTP-status-code-only testing.

**BUG (severe, fixed)**: `MockLLMProvider`'s JSON-mode branch (`src/lib/providers/llm/mock.provider.ts`) had no awareness of `lib/creative/scene-split.ts`'s request shape — it fell through to `simulateUniversalPromptJson()`'s unrelated shape (no `scenes` field), failing `sceneSplitSchema` validation every time. Confirmed live: `POST /api/videos` failed with `Scene-split response did not match the expected shape` on a genuinely clean, zero-provider-rows database — meaning **any founder using the default Mock LLM (i.e., anyone who hasn't yet configured a real provider) could never successfully create a single video project.** Fixed by adding a `Script:\n`-prefix-matching branch that returns a valid `{ scenes: [...], textOverlays: [] }` shape. Verified via a real rebuild + retest: project creation now succeeds end-to-end (`status: "SCRIPT_READY"`, real generated script text returned).

**Bug investigated, found to be by-design, not fixed**: a real `POST /api/assets/upload` attempt (production mode, no storage provider configured — the wizard's own "Local storage (dev)" default) threw `StorageProviderUnavailableError`, confirming `getStorageProvider()`'s 2026-07-23 hard-refuse-in-production behavior is real and reachable, not just theoretical. This is intentional (matches Payment's identical posture — no silent Mock fallback for either in production, a deliberate anti-exploit/anti-data-loss decision), so left unchanged.

**Bug found in that same investigation (minor, fixed)**: the Launch-Readiness checklist's warning text (`lib/admin/installation-status.ts`) claimed every unconfigured category was "falling back to the mock provider" — factually wrong for STORAGE and PAYMENT specifically, which hard-refuse instead. A founder reading this warning could reasonably (and incorrectly) conclude it's non-urgent. Fixed the wording for those two categories only; the other 6 categories' message was already accurate.

**Also verified, no issues found**: full 15-step flow (create admin → configure storage/AI providers → seed → finish → onboarding submission with real session `update()` refresh → dashboard → logout → login again via the password provider → project creation → settings review → repeated browser refresh) all behave correctly. Session persists correctly across a full server *restart* (stronger proof than a mere page refresh — confirms the JWT is genuinely stateless, not dependent on any in-memory server state). `/settings` was found to be a read-only summary page with no separate save action in the current app — not a bug, just clarifying what "save settings" maps to today (the onboarding profile-update path, already covered).

**Verification**: `tsc --noEmit`, `eslint`, `vitest run` (135/135, 3330/3330), and `npm run build` all clean after both fixes. All temporary test artifacts (database, cookie jars, standalone static-asset copies) cleaned up; `.env.local` restored to the real dev database.
